questions.stem: A researcher examines developing lymphocytes in the bone marrow. One cell has successfully rearranged and expresses a mu heavy chain, but this chain is paired with an invariant surrogate light chain rather than a true, rearranged light chain. Light chain gene rearrangement has not yet been completed. This cell is at which stage of B cell maturation?

explanation.summary: The pre-B cell expresses a mu heavy chain paired with a surrogate light chain, forming the pre-BCR.
explanation.whyCorrect: By definition, a pre-B cell has produced a functional VH domain and expresses the mu heavy chain paired with a surrogate (non-rearranged) light chain. This complex is the pre-BCR. If the pre-BCR signals successfully, the cell then begins light chain VJ recombination.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Immature B cells have already rearranged a true light chain and express a complete surface IgM (BCR), not a surrogate light chain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mature naive B cells have completed selection and express surface IgM and IgD, not a pre-BCR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated antibody-secreting effector cells generated after activation, not a bone-marrow maturation stage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pro-B cells are only beginning heavy chain VDJ recombination and do not yet express a mu chain or any receptor.

questions.stem: Humans are diploid and carry two alleles for the immunoglobulin heavy chain locus, yet a single mature B cell expresses B-cell receptors derived from only one of these alleles. At the pre-B cell stage, successful signaling through the pre-BCR shuts down further rearrangement of the second allele. Which process does this describe?

explanation.summary: Allelic exclusion ensures each B cell expresses BCRs from only one immunoglobulin allele.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although B cells are diploid, allelic exclusion guarantees that only one allele is productively used. When the pre-BCR signals at the pre-B cell stage, the cell silences rearrangement of the other allele; if no signal occurs, the cell undergoes apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Negative selection removes strongly self-reactive cells; it does not govern which allele is expressed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Positive selection tests whether the assembled BCR is functional, allowing weakly self-binding cells to mature.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptor editing rescues autoreactive immature B cells by rearranging the other light chain gene, not by ensuring single-allele expression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatic hypermutation introduces mutations into the BCR variable region during the germinal center reaction, long after this stage.

questions.stem: An immature B cell in the bone marrow expresses a newly assembled BCR that binds a self-antigen with high affinity. Rather than being deleted, the cell undergoes a second round of VJ recombination at its other light chain constant gene (lambda), generating a new receptor that no longer reacts to self. Which mechanism has rescued this cell?

explanation.summary: Receptor editing lets a self-reactive immature B cell rearrange its other light chain gene to escape deletion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Immature B cells carry two light chain constant genes (kappa and lambda) but initially express only one. If strong self-antigen recognition occurs, the cell can perform VJ recombination on the other gene; expression of the new light chain gives it a second pass through selection. About 25% of circulating B cells show evidence of receptor editing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Allelic exclusion silences the second allele of the same chain and does not create a new, non-self-reactive receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Negative selection with apoptosis is exactly what receptor editing allows the cell to avoid; here the cell survives.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Positive selection simply allows weakly self-binding, functional BCRs to mature; it does not remodel the receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatic hypermutation occurs in the germinal center dark zone during affinity maturation, not in the bone marrow.

questions.stem: A B cell has just completed selection in the bone marrow and been released into the circulation as a mature, naive cell that has not yet encountered antigen. Which pair of immunoglobulin isotypes is displayed on its surface?

explanation.summary: Mature naive B cells co-express surface IgM and IgD.
explanation.whyCorrect: Naive B cells express both the mu and delta heavy chain constant domains, so their membranes display both IgM and IgD. This distinguishes them from immature B cells, which express surface IgM alone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA is a class-switched isotype (directed by TGF-beta and BAFF) and is not present on naive cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgG and IgE are both class-switched isotypes seen only after activation, not on a naive B cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgG appears only after class switching in an antigen-driven germinal center reaction, not on naive cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Surface IgM alone characterizes the immature B cell, before the delta chain is co-expressed.

questions.stem: Sixteen days after an emergency splenectomy, a 54-year-old man develops body aches, nasal congestion, fever, low platelets, and a high white blood cell count. He rapidly progresses to sepsis and dies within 20 hours despite broad-spectrum antibiotics; blood cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae. Loss of which splenic function best explains his overwhelming susceptibility to this encapsulated organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow maturation of new B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Germinal center formation in the lymph nodes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thymic education of self-tolerant T cells

explanation.summary: Splenectomy removes the marginal-zone/B1 cells and blood-filtering that opsonize encapsulated bacteria.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen filters blood and houses marginal-zone and B1 cells that provide natural IgM against blood-borne antigens; splenic loss lowers serum IgM and impairs complement-mediated opsonization. Because complement and opsonization are the main defense against encapsulated organisms, asplenic patients are prone to overwhelming post-splenectomy infection. Vaccination against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type B before elective splenectomy can prevent this.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells still mature normally in the bone marrow after splenectomy; the deficit is in blood filtering and marginal-zone antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymph node germinal centers remain intact after splenectomy and are not the basis of encapsulated-organism defense.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The spleen is not the site of neutrophil production, and his white count was actually elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: T cell tolerance is established in the thymus, not the spleen, and is unrelated to this infection.

questions.stem: During an episode of gram-negative bacteremia, bacterial antigens circulate in the bloodstream. Which secondary lymphoid site is chiefly responsible for filtering these blood-borne antigens and presenting them to lymphocytes?

explanation.summary: The spleen filters blood, and its marginal-zone macrophages capture blood-borne antigens for presentation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Blood-borne antigens are filtered in the spleen. In the marginal zone between red and white pulp, macrophages capture these antigens and present them to lymphocytes, including marginal-zone B cells. This is the key difference from lymph nodes, whose antigens arrive via the lymphatics.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bone marrow is the site of B cell maturation, not a filter for blood-borne antigen presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The lymph node paracortex is a T cell zone that samples antigens arriving through lymphatics, not blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peyer patches sample antigens transferred across the intestinal epithelium, not circulating blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thymic medulla is involved in T cell development and negative selection, not blood filtering.

questions.stem: A naive lymphocyte circulating in the blood must leave the vasculature to enter a lymph node. After L-selectin-mediated rolling and integrin-mediated adhesion, through which specialized vascular structure does it cross the endothelium to enter the node?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Afferent lymphatic vessels of the node

choices.label: B
choices.text: Central arterioles of the white pulp

choices.label: C
choices.text: Efferent lymphatic vessels of the node

choices.label: E
choices.text: The thoracic duct in the chest

explanation.summary: Lymphocytes enter lymph nodes from the blood through high endothelial venules.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymphocyte trafficking mirrors neutrophil trafficking: L-selectin mediates rolling, integrins such as LFA-1 bind CAMs for adhesion, and PECAM-1 mediates diapedesis. Lymphocytes then enter the lymph node through specialized high endothelial venules (HEVs).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Afferent lymphatics carry antigen and fluid into the node; naive lymphocytes enter from blood, not lymph.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Central arterioles are a landmark of the splenic white pulp (PALS), not the lymphocyte entry portal of a lymph node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Efferent lymphatics carry effector cells out of the node, not into it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The thoracic duct returns lymph to the bloodstream and is not the site of entry into a node.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections. Laboratory studies show a markedly elevated serum IgM but very low IgG, IgA, and IgE, and lymph node biopsy reveals absent germinal centers. His B cells recognize antigen, internalize it, and present peptide on MHC II normally. A defect in which interaction best explains why his B cells cannot class switch or enter the germinal center reaction?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Somatic hypermutation in the dark zone

explanation.summary: The CD40-CD40L signal from helper T cells is required for B cells to enter the germinal center and class switch.
explanation.whyCorrect: In T-dependent activation, after the B cell presents peptide on MHC II, the CD40-CD40L interaction further activates the B cell and allows it to enter the germinal center reaction, where class switching occurs. Without this signal, B cells cannot class switch or form germinal centers, so they secrete only IgM, producing high IgM with low IgG/IgA/IgE.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCR crosslinking is intact here (the B cells recognize and internalize antigen); it alone cannot drive class switching without T cell help.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L-selectin governs lymphocyte homing to lymph nodes, not class switching or germinal center formation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B cells present antigen on MHC class II to CD4+ helper T cells, not MHC class I; his MHC II presentation is described as normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatic hypermutation mediates affinity maturation and is downstream of the CD40 signal; it does not by itself explain the absent germinal centers and isotype defect.

questions.stem: A purified bacterial capsular polysaccharide vaccine is administered to a patient. The response consists only of low-affinity IgM, with no class switching, no affinity maturation, and no lasting memory. This limited response reflects which type of B cell activation?

explanation.summary: Multivalent polysaccharides drive T-independent activation, yielding low-affinity IgM without memory.
explanation.whyCorrect: Non-protein antigens such as polysaccharides cannot be presented on MHC II, so they activate B cells without T cell help. Their repeated, identical epitopes crosslink many BCRs; combined with signals like PRR or CR2-C3d binding, this activates the cell. Because these cells receive no T cell help and are not allowed into the germinal center, they make low-affinity IgM and undergo no affinity maturation or class switching.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Negative selection is a bone-marrow tolerance mechanism that removes autoreactive cells, not a response to vaccination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Positive selection tests BCR functionality during maturation and is unrelated to the antibody response to a vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: T-dependent activation requires a protein antigen and CD4+ helper T cell participation, producing class-switched, high-affinity antibody and memory.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The germinal center reaction is precisely what T-independent responses do NOT enter, which is why there is no affinity maturation or class switching.

questions.stem: An infant is given a Haemophilus influenzae type B vaccine in which the capsular polysaccharide is covalently linked to a protein carrier. Unlike the pure polysaccharide vaccine, this conjugate elicits high-affinity, class-switched IgG and durable memory. What is the mechanistic basis for this improved response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The B cell presents peptides from the carrier protein on MHC II

choices.label: B
choices.text: The carrier acts as a superantigen that bypasses antigen specificity

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conjugate crosslinks BCRs so strongly that no T cell help is needed

choices.label: D
choices.text: The conjugate triggers somatic hypermutation directly in the bone marrow

choices.label: E
choices.text: The polysaccharide directly activates helper T cells

explanation.summary: Conjugation lets a polysaccharide-specific B cell present carrier peptides to T cells, converting the response to T-dependent.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a conjugate vaccine, a BCR specific for the polysaccharide binds and internalizes the conjugate, then processes and presents peptides from the linked protein on MHC II. A helper T cell specific for that peptide provides help, so the B cell now receives the germinal center signals needed to make high-affinity, class-switched, polysaccharide-specific IgG and memory.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The carrier is a conventional protein antigen presented in a peptide-specific manner, not a superantigen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The benefit comes precisely from recruiting T cell help via the carrier peptide, not from bypassing it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatic hypermutation occurs in the germinal center of secondary lymphoid organs, not in the bone marrow, and is downstream of T cell help.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Polysaccharides cannot be presented on MHC II and do not directly activate T cells; that is exactly why the plain polysaccharide is poorly immunogenic.

questions.stem: A patient presents with diarrhea, and stool ova-and-parasite examination reveals a helminth infection. In the germinal center response to this pathogen, which cytokine secreted by follicular helper T cells directs B cells to class switch to IgE?

explanation.summary: IL-4 from follicular helper T cells drives class switching to IgE, the antibody of antiparasitic responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the light zone, follicular helper T cells secrete cytokines that direct which class a B cell switches to. IL-4 promotes switching to IgE, which is well suited to parasitic infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma directs class switching to IgG, not IgE.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-2 is a T cell growth factor and is not the cytokine that directs the IgE class switch in this context.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TGF-beta together with BAFF directs switching to IgA, important at mucosal surfaces.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine that causes fever and does not direct class switching to IgE.

questions.stem: In a germinal center, a B cell rapidly divides and acquires point mutations in the complementarity-determining regions of its BCR within the dark zone, then migrates to the light zone where it must compete for antigen displayed on follicular dendritic cells; only the highest-affinity clones receive survival signals and persist. This coupled cycle of mutation and selection accomplishes which overall outcome?

explanation.summary: Somatic hypermutation in the dark zone plus FDC-based selection in the light zone yields affinity maturation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dark-zone B cells undergo somatic hypermutation, introducing mutations into the CDR/hypervariable regions. In the light zone, B cells with the highest-affinity BCRs outcompete others for antigen on follicular dendritic cells and receive survival signals, while low-affinity cells apoptose. Iterating this mutation-and-selection cycle progressively raises antibody affinity, the definition of affinity maturation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Class switching, mediated by AID deleting DNA between constant-region genes, changes the antibody isotype, not its affinity for antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Negative selection removes self-reactive cells during maturation; germinal center selection here is based on antigen affinity, not autoreactivity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptor editing is a bone-marrow tolerance mechanism in immature B cells, not a germinal center affinity process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VDJ recombination assembles the original variable region in the bone marrow and is not the germinal center process described.

questions.stem: A bone marrow sample is analyzed by flow cytometry and PCR. One population of lymphoid precursors expresses no immunoglobulin of any kind on its surface, yet analysis of its DNA shows that immunoglobulin heavy chain V, D, and J gene segments are actively being joined. These cells are at which stage of B cell maturation?

explanation.summary: Pro-B cells are beginning heavy chain VDJ recombination and express no form of the BCR.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pro-B cell is the first stage of B cell development. At this stage the developing B cell begins rearranging heavy chain gene segments by VDJ recombination, but no receptor of any kind is yet displayed on the surface. Only after a VH domain is successfully generated does the cell express the mu heavy chain and become a pre-B cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hematopoietic stem cells are the multipotent precursors of all lymphoid cells; they are not yet committed to the B lineage and are not rearranging immunoglobulin genes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immature B cells have rearranged both heavy and light chains and express a complete surface IgM BCR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mature naive B cells have passed selection and display both IgM and IgD on their surface.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pre-B cells have already completed heavy chain rearrangement and display the mu chain with a surrogate light chain as the pre-BCR.

questions.stem: Developing B cells from a patient reach the stage at which a mu heavy chain is displayed with a surrogate light chain, and signaling through this receptor occurs normally. However, no cells ever progress to express a complete surface IgM molecule. Failure of recombination of which of the following gene segments best explains this arrest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heavy chain V, D, and J segments

choices.label: B
choices.text: Light chain V and J segments

choices.label: C
choices.text: The delta heavy chain constant gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gamma heavy chain constant gene

explanation.summary: The checkpoint from pre-B to immature B cell is successful light chain VJ recombination and expression of a complete IgM BCR.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once the pre-BCR signals, light chain VJ recombination begins. An immature B cell is defined by expression of a rearranged light chain paired with the mu heavy chain to form a complete BCR. If the light chain V and J segments cannot recombine, no true light chain is made and the cells cannot progress beyond the pre-B stage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heavy chain VDJ recombination was clearly successful, because the cells already display a mu heavy chain in the pre-BCR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The delta constant domain is co-expressed only in mature naive B cells to produce IgD; it is not needed to form the complete IgM BCR of the immature B cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The gamma constant gene is used only after class switching in the germinal center; it plays no role in bone marrow maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The surrogate light chain is functioning, as shown by normal pre-BCR assembly and signaling; it is the true light chain that never appears.

questions.stem: A developing B cell in the bone marrow assembles a mu heavy chain, but the chain fails to pair with the surrogate light chain, so no signal is transmitted through the pre-BCR. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this cell?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Differentiation into a short-lived plasma cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Initiation of light chain VJ recombination

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receptor editing at the lambda light chain gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release into the circulation expressing IgD alone

explanation.summary: At the pre-B cell checkpoint, absence of pre-BCR signaling leads to apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pre-BCR is tested at the pre-B cell stage. If signaling occurs, the cell shuts off rearrangement of the other allele and proceeds; if signaling does not occur, the B cell goes through apoptosis. A mu chain that cannot form a functional pre-BCR therefore cannot rescue the cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Plasma cells arise only after a mature B cell is activated by antigen in a secondary lymphoid organ.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Light chain VJ recombination begins only if the pre-BCR is functional and signals; here no signal is delivered.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptor editing is a rescue for immature B cells that fail negative selection because of strong self-reactivity, not for pre-B cells lacking a functional pre-BCR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cells cannot be released without passing all checkpoints, and mature naive B cells express IgM together with IgD, never IgD alone.

questions.stem: An immature B cell in the bone marrow displays a complete IgM BCR. Because the marrow is a sterile environment, the receptor is tested against self-antigens rather than foreign antigens, and it binds these self-antigens only weakly. Which of the following is the most likely outcome for this cell?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maturation and release into the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Receptor editing of the light chain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Retention in the marrow as a pro-B cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Silencing of the second heavy chain allele

explanation.summary: Weak binding to self-antigen is the positive selection signal that a BCR is functional, allowing the B cell to mature.
explanation.whyCorrect: Positive selection tests BCRs for function. Because the bone marrow is sterile and foreign antigens are unavailable, self-antigens are presented to immature B cells. If the BCR binds weakly, the immune system knows the receptor is functional, and the B cell is allowed to mature, migrate to the periphery, and circulate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Negative selection and apoptosis are triggered by strong autoreactivity, not by the weak self-binding that indicates a functional receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptor editing is a second chance for cells that show strong self-antigen recognition; a weakly binding, functional BCR does not need editing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This cell has already progressed well beyond the pro-B stage, since it expresses a complete BCR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Allelic exclusion occurs earlier, at the pre-B stage, when pre-BCR signaling shuts off rearrangement of the other allele.

questions.stem: In an experimental model, immature B cells whose BCRs bind self-antigen strongly are neither deleted nor able to rearrange an alternative light chain, and they are released into the periphery as mature cells. Which of the following is the most likely consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of surface IgD on mature B cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure to respond to polysaccharide antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inability of B cells to form germinal centers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of allelic exclusion at the heavy chain locus

explanation.summary: Negative selection prevents release of autoreactive B cells; when it fails, those cells can activate and generate autoantibodies.
explanation.whyCorrect: Negative selection tests BCRs for self-reactivity. If an autoreactive B cell is released, it can activate, proliferate, and generate autoantibodies directed against self-antigens. Normally immature B cells with strong autoreactivity undergo apoptosis unless receptor editing rescues them; in this model both safeguards are bypassed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Co-expression of IgD with IgM in naive B cells depends on the delta constant domain, not on negative selection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: T-independent responses to multivalent polysaccharides require BCR crosslinking and co-stimulation, which remain intact in these cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Germinal center entry depends on antigen recognition and CD40-CD40L T cell help, which are not affected by a tolerance defect.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Allelic exclusion is established at the pre-B stage by pre-BCR signaling and is independent of the selection of immature B cells.

questions.stem: A naive B cell circulating in the blood rolls along the endothelium of a specialized venule in a lymph node, becomes firmly adherent, and then squeezes between endothelial cells to enter the node. Which of the following molecules mediates this final step of diapedesis?

explanation.summary: Lymphocyte diapedesis through the endothelium is mediated by PECAM-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymphocyte trafficking mirrors neutrophil trafficking. L-selectins mediate rolling on endothelial cells, cytokines and chemokines activate integrins like LFA-1, the integrins bind endothelial cell adhesion molecules (CAMs) for firm adhesion, and PECAM-1 mediates diapedesis, the movement between endothelial cells into the tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD40 is displayed by activated B cells and binds CD40L on helper T cells; it has no role in endothelial transmigration.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CR2 is the B cell receptor for the complement fragment C3d, a co-stimulatory signal for activation, not a trafficking molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L-selectin mediates the initial rolling of the lymphocyte on the endothelium, not its passage through the vessel wall.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LFA-1 is the integrin that binds endothelial CAMs to produce firm adhesion, the step before diapedesis.

questions.stem: In an experimental animal, naive lymphocytes are rendered unable to bind the L-selectin ligands displayed on high endothelial venules. Naive B cell entry into which of the following sites would be expected to remain intact?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Germinal centers of a lymph node

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medullary cords of a lymph node

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary follicles of a lymph node

explanation.summary: B cells enter the spleen directly through its open circulatory system, so splenic entry does not depend on HEVs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymphocytes enter lymph nodes through high endothelial venules, which have high expression of L-selectin ligands and CAMs. The spleen is different: its red pulp contains an open circulatory system, and B cells can directly enter the spleen through this open circulation without crossing HEVs. Loss of L-selectin binding therefore blocks lymph node entry but spares the spleen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Germinal centers form inside lymph node follicles and are reached only by B cells that first entered the node via HEVs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The medullary cords lie within the lymph node, which lymphocytes can no longer enter from the blood in this model.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The paracortex contains the HEVs themselves; entry into it from the blood depends on L-selectin binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B cells reach the primary follicles of the lymph node cortex only after entering the node through HEVs, which requires L-selectin-mediated rolling.

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy from a patient with an active infection shows cortical follicles that are less densely packed than usual and contain central areas of proliferating cells. Which of the following best describes these structures?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary follicles containing quiescent B cells

explanation.summary: Activated primary follicles become secondary follicles, which are less densely packed and may contain germinal centers.
explanation.whyCorrect: B cells initially reside in the lymph node cortex as densely packed, quiescent cells in primary follicles. On activation, primary follicles develop into secondary follicles, which are active, less densely packed, and may contain germinal centers, the specialized structures that mediate affinity maturation and isotype switching.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The marginal zone is a splenic structure between red and white pulp, not a component of the lymph node cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Medullary cords are part of the medulla through which effector cells exit; they are not cortical follicles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The paracortex is the T cell zone beneath the cortex and does not form follicles with germinal centers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Primary follicles are densely packed and quiescent; the loose packing and central proliferation described indicate activation.

questions.stem: A naive B cell and a naive T cell cross the same high endothelial venule into a lymph node. Shortly afterward, the B cell has localized to a follicle in the cortex while the T cell has remained in the paracortex. Which of the following directs each cell to its respective compartment?

explanation.summary: After entry through HEVs, chemokines guide B cells to the cortex and T cells to the paracortex.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary lymphoid organs segregate lymphocytes into compartments. In lymph nodes, B cells are found in the cortex and T cells in the paracortex, which also contains the HEVs and the dendritic cells that activate T cells. Chemokines guide B and T cells to their respective regions after entry via HEVs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BCR crosslinking is an activation signal delivered by antigen; naive cells localize to their zones before encountering antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD40-CD40L is the interaction between an activated B cell and a helper T cell that permits germinal center entry, not a positioning cue for naive cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: L-selectin mediates rolling on the HEV endothelium before entry; it does not sort cells within the node.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PECAM-1 mediates diapedesis across the endothelium, a step completed before the cells are positioned in the node.

questions.stem: After activation in a lymph node, an effector B cell leaves the node to return to the blood. Which of the following correctly orders the structures it passes through?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Afferent lymphatic, cortex, high endothelial venule

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medulla, high endothelial venule, efferent lymphatic

choices.label: E
choices.text: Paracortex, high endothelial venule, thoracic duct

explanation.summary: Effector lymphocytes exit the lymph node via the medulla and efferent lymphatics, then reach the blood through the thoracic duct.
explanation.whyCorrect: Effector B and T cells leave the lymph nodes via the medulla and then the efferent lymph vessel(s). Lymph from the efferent lymphatics is carried by the thoracic duct back into the blood circulation, from which the cells can reach tissues or other secondary lymphoid organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Afferent lymphatics carry antigen and fluid into the node, and HEVs are the entry portal for naive cells from the blood; neither is an exit route.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Afferent lymphatics deliver lymph into the node; cells do not exit through them.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HEVs are not part of the exit pathway; cells move from the medulla into the efferent lymphatic directly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HEVs are for entry, not exit, and cells do not pass from an HEV directly into the thoracic duct.

questions.stem: A histologic section of spleen shows a central arteriole surrounded by a cuff of lymphocytes, which is in turn surrounded by lymphoid follicles. The lymphocytes immediately around the arteriole are predominantly which of the following?

explanation.summary: The periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS) around splenic central arterioles is the T cell zone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within the white pulp of the spleen, T cells are found in the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath (PALS), the area immediately around central arterioles. The canonical B cells are found in follicles surrounding the PALS.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B1 cells reside in the marginal zone between the red and white pulp, not around the central arteriole.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Canonical B cells occupy the follicles that surround the PALS, not the sheath immediately around the arteriole.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Macrophages that capture blood-borne antigens are located in the marginal zone, not in the PALS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Plasma cells are antibody-secreting effector cells generated after activation and are not the defining population of the PALS.

questions.stem: A pathologist examining the spleen identifies a region that contains an open circulatory system and functions primarily to filter the blood rather than to house lymphocytes. Which of the following is this region?

explanation.summary: The red pulp of the spleen contains an open circulatory system and filters blood; the white pulp holds most of the lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spleen is composed of red pulp and white pulp. Red pulp contains an open circulatory system and filters blood, while white pulp contains most of the lymphocytes. The marginal zone lies between the two, where macrophages capture blood-borne antigens for presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Follicles are the B cell zones of the white pulp surrounding the PALS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Germinal centers are structures within activated follicles that mediate affinity maturation and isotype switching, not blood filtration.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The PALS is the T cell zone within the white pulp, immediately around central arterioles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The white pulp is the lymphocyte-rich compartment (PALS and follicles), not the blood-filtering region.

questions.stem: Blood-borne bacterial antigen is captured by macrophages in the splenic marginal zone, and the B cells residing in this zone respond rapidly by producing antibody. Compared with the canonical B cells of the follicles, these marginal zone B cells are characterized by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A lower activation threshold and predominant IgM secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: A strict requirement for Tfh cell help before activation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Extensive affinity maturation within germinal centers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Migration to the PALS after antigen encounter

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preferential class switching to IgA under TGF-beta

explanation.summary: Marginal zone (B1) B cells have a lower activation threshold, stay in the marginal zone, receive no T cell help, and predominantly secrete IgM.
explanation.whyCorrect: A specialized population of B cells, called MZ B cells or B1 cells, resides in the marginal zone between red and white pulp. B1 cells have a lower activation threshold than canonical B cells. They do not migrate outside of the marginal zone and do not receive T cell help, so they predominantly secrete IgM.

whyWrongByChoice.B: B1 cells do not receive T cell help; a requirement for Tfh help is a feature of canonical B cells undergoing T-dependent activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Affinity maturation requires the germinal center reaction, which B1 cells do not enter because they never leave the marginal zone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: B1 cells do not migrate outside the marginal zone; the PALS is the T cell zone of the white pulp.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Class switching to IgA requires Tfh cytokines in the germinal center light zone; B1 cells lack T cell help and remain IgM producers.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is scheduled to undergo an elective splenectomy in 6 weeks. Which of the following is the most appropriate step to reduce his risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administration of IFN-gamma to boost IgG after surgery

choices.label: B
choices.text: Administration of IVIG on the day of surgery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Transfusion of donor IgM immediately after surgery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vaccination against encapsulated bacteria before surgery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaccination against tetanus toxin after surgery

explanation.summary: Before a planned splenectomy, patients should be vaccinated against S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, and H. influenzae type B.
explanation.whyCorrect: When a splenectomy is planned, the patient should be vaccinated against Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type B, the three encapsulated organisms most commonly responsible for overwhelming post-splenectomy infection. Conjugate vaccines given before splenectomy convert the capsular polysaccharide into a T-dependent antigen, generating high-affinity memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells that secrete protective IgG, so protection is in place before splenic filtering and B1 cells are lost.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma directs class switching to IgG within germinal centers; it is not a clinical intervention that substitutes for vaccination against specific pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IVIG provides only temporary passive antibody and can actually block generation of memory by competing for antigen in germinal centers; it does not create lasting protection against encapsulated organisms.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Transfusing IgM is not a described strategy; the goal is to induce the patient's own high-affinity IgG and memory against the specific encapsulated bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tetanus is not among the encapsulated organisms that cause post-splenectomy sepsis, and vaccinating after surgery misses the opportunity to have protection in place beforehand.

questions.stem: During a bacterial infection, complement is activated and fragments of C3 are deposited on the bacterial surface. A naive B cell binds a bacterial antigen through its BCR, and a second receptor on the same B cell simultaneously binds the deposited fragment C3d, providing a co-stimulatory signal. Which of the following is this second receptor?

explanation.summary: CR2 binding to the complement fragment C3d supplies a co-stimulatory signal for B cell activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: For optimal B cell activation, the B cell must receive an inflammatory signal in addition to BCR crosslinking. That co-stimulatory signal may be TLR binding to PAMPs or CR2 binding to a fragment of complement, C3d. Here the ligand is specified as C3d, so the receptor is CR2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD40 on the activated B cell binds CD40L on a helper T cell; it does not bind complement.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LFA-1 is an integrin that binds endothelial CAMs for firm adhesion during trafficking.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class II presents processed peptide to CD4+ helper T cells; it is not a complement receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TLRs deliver an alternative co-stimulatory signal by binding PAMPs, not the complement fragment C3d.

questions.stem: A naive B cell in a lymph node follicle has bound and internalized a protein antigen by receptor-mediated endocytosis and now displays peptide-MHC class II complexes and CD40 on its surface. To which of the following locations does this cell migrate next in order to obtain T cell help?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A high endothelial venule within the paracortex

choices.label: B
choices.text: The border of the B cell and T cell zones

choices.label: C
choices.text: The center of the follicle to seed a germinal center

choices.label: D
choices.text: The efferent lymphatic vessel leaving the medulla

choices.label: E
choices.text: The medullary sinus draining toward the efferent vessel

explanation.summary: Activated B cells migrate to the border of the B and T cell zones to encounter a Tfh cell with a matching TCR.
explanation.whyCorrect: After processing antigen, activated B cells display both peptide-MHC class II complexes and CD40 on their surface. They migrate to the border of the B and T cell zones, where they may encounter a CD4+ follicular helper T cell whose TCR is specific for their peptide-MHC class II complex. This immunological synapse provides the additional activation help.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HEVs are the entry portal for naive lymphocytes from the blood; the B cell is already inside the node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B cells migrate to the center of the follicle to seed a germinal center only after they have received T cell help at the zone border.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The efferent lymphatic carries effector cells out of the node; the B cell has not yet been fully activated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The medullary sinus is part of the exit pathway for effector cells, not the site of T cell help.

questions.stem: Five days after a first exposure to a protein antigen, a patient's serum already contains antigen-specific IgM, although lymph node biopsy shows no germinal centers yet. Which of the following cells is the most likely source of this early antibody?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Light zone germinal center B cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Memory B cells in the follicle

explanation.summary: Short-lived extrafollicular plasma cells secrete the first wave of IgM before the germinal center is established.
explanation.whyCorrect: After receiving T cell help at the border of the B and T cell zones, some B cells differentiate into short-lived extrafollicular plasma cells. These produce antibodies in the early immune response, before the GC is established, and then undergo apoptosis. In a primary response, these extrafollicular plasma cells secrete IgM; IgG appears later as germinal centers form.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Follicular dendritic cells hold antigen on their surface for B cell selection; they do not secrete antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Light zone B cells are germinal center cells competing for antigen on FDCs; no germinal centers have yet formed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Long-lived plasma cells are a product of the germinal center reaction and account for persisting IgG late in the response, not early IgM.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Memory B cells are generated during the response and remain quiescent until re-exposure; in a first exposure they cannot be the source of day-5 antibody.

questions.stem: Within a few weeks of an infection, up to 10% of a patient's total B cell population is specific for the pathogen. Two months after the pathogen has been cleared, only a small fraction of these cells remains. Which of the following best explains the loss of most of the pathogen-specific B cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow release of naive B cells is halted until numbers fall

choices.label: B
choices.text: Class switching to IgG causes the cells to leave the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Follicular dendritic cells actively kill B cells no longer bound to antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of BCR engagement lets upregulated apoptosis signals prevail

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptor editing changes the specificity of the expanded clones

explanation.summary: Activated B cells upregulate apoptosis signals and depend on BCR engagement; once antigen is gone, apoptosis wins.
explanation.whyCorrect: B cell proliferation during infection is extensive, yet the total number of B cells remains relatively constant. Naive B cells, activated B cells, and most plasma cells must receive signals through the BCR to survive, and activated B cells upregulate apoptosis signals. Without BCR engagement after antigen is cleared, the apoptosis signals win and the cells go through apoptosis, contracting the response to make room for new B cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The bone marrow continually releases naive B cells; homeostasis is achieved by apoptosis of activated cells, not by halting marrow output.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Class switching changes the antibody isotype and does not remove cells from the body; the contraction is due to cell death.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FDCs provide survival signals to B cells that access antigen in the light zone; they do not actively kill cells, and the loss described is passive apoptosis from lack of survival signals.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor editing is a bone-marrow tolerance mechanism in immature B cells; it does not occur in expanded peripheral clones after infection.

questions.stem: Long-lived plasma cells and memory B cells require fewer survival signals than other B cells and upregulate anti-apoptotic genes, yet their total numbers remain small and relatively constant across a lifetime of immune responses. Which of the following best explains this limit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An ongoing requirement for CD40-CD40L signaling from follicular helper T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Competition for survival signals within limited niches such as the bone marrow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Continuous negative selection against self-reactive plasma cells in the periphery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dependence on repeated BCR crosslinking by multivalent polysaccharide antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Progressive receptor editing that eliminates the highest-affinity clones

explanation.summary: Only small numbers of memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells are produced, and they compete for survival signals in limited niches.
explanation.whyCorrect: Memory B cells and long-lived plasma cells need fewer signals to survive and upregulate anti-apoptotic genes, but only a small number are produced in any immune response. Those that are produced still compete with each other for survival signals, and this competition occurs in small niches with limited space, such as long-lived plasma cell competition within the bone marrow.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD40-CD40L signaling is required for germinal center entry, not for the ongoing survival of long-lived plasma cells, which need fewer signals than other B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Negative selection is a bone-marrow checkpoint for immature B cells; it is not described as a continuous process pruning plasma cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Long-lived plasma cells and memory cells are products of T-dependent responses; BCR crosslinking by polysaccharide is the trigger of T-independent activation, not a survival requirement here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor editing occurs in immature B cells in the bone marrow and rescues self-reactive cells; it does not eliminate high-affinity effector clones.

questions.stem: A light zone B cell in a germinal center converts from producing IgM to producing IgA. This change requires deletion of the DNA encoding the mu and delta constant domains so that the rearranged VH gene is spliced to the alpha constant domain gene. Which of the following directly mediates this deletion?

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD40 ligand on the helper T cell

explanation.summary: Activation-induced deaminase (AID) deletes DNA between constant domain genes to accomplish class switching.
explanation.whyCorrect: B cells in the light zone express activation-induced deaminase (AID), an enzyme that deletes the DNA between constant domain genes. In this way a B cell can delete mu and delta, splicing the variable domain (VH) genes to the gamma, alpha, or epsilon constant domain genes. Tfh cytokines determine which class is chosen, but AID performs the deletion itself.

whyWrongByChoice.B: BAFF acts together with TGF-beta to promote the IgA switch; like TGF-beta it is a directing signal, not the enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD40 ligand on the Tfh cell binds CD40 to allow the B cell to enter the germinal center reaction; it does not mediate DNA deletion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Follicular dendritic cells hold antigen and provide survival signals to high-affinity B cells; they play no role in cutting the constant region DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TGF-beta is a Tfh cytokine that promotes switching to IgA; it directs the choice of class but does not itself cut DNA.

questions.stem: A germinal center B cell in the light zone is exposed to TGF-beta and BAFF secreted by follicular helper T cells. After class switching, its rearranged VH gene will be spliced to which of the following heavy chain constant domain genes?

explanation.summary: TGF-beta and BAFF direct class switching to IgA, which uses the alpha heavy chain constant domain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tfh cells in the light zone secrete cytokines that promote switching to specific classes: IFN-gamma promotes switching to IgG, IL-4 to IgE, and TGF-beta and BAFF to IgA. Switching to IgA means AID deletes mu and delta and the VH gene is spliced to the alpha constant domain gene.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The delta constant domain encodes IgD of the naive B cell and is deleted along with mu during switching.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The epsilon constant domain produces IgE, the switch promoted by IL-4.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The gamma constant domain produces IgG, the switch promoted by IFN-gamma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The mu constant domain encodes IgM; it is deleted, not retained, during class switching.

questions.stem: Fifty-six days after a single primary immunization, a patient's serum contains almost no antigen-specific IgM, but a low, stable level of antigen-specific IgG persists. Which of the following cells produces this persisting IgG?

explanation.summary: Once a primary response has contracted, any remaining serum IgG comes from long-lived plasma cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a primary immune response, extrafollicular plasma cells first secrete IgM, and more IgG is made as germinal centers form. As antigen is cleared, the response slows, the short-lived plasma cells go through apoptosis, and memory B cells remain quiescent. Any remaining serum IgG is from long-lived plasma cells, which are products of the germinal center reaction.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B1 cells reside in the splenic marginal zone and predominantly secrete IgM, not class-switched IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dark zone B cells are rapidly dividing germinal center cells undergoing somatic hypermutation; they are not antibody-secreting cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extrafollicular plasma cells are short-lived, secrete IgM early in the response, and have undergone apoptosis by this time.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Memory B cells remain quiescent and do not secrete antibody unless reactivated by their antigen.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man who has never been immunized against tetanus sustains a contaminated wound and is given intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) purified from healthy donors, which neutralizes the toxin and prevents illness. He is instructed to return in several weeks for tetanus vaccination. Which of the following best explains why the IVIG itself does not leave him with lasting immunity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IVIG binds antigen on FDCs so cognate B cells fail to survive the GC reaction

choices.label: B
choices.text: IVIG blocks L-selectin binding so B cells cannot enter lymph nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: IVIG crosslinks BCRs and drives only a T-independent IgM response

choices.label: D
choices.text: IVIG is cleared from the blood before reaching secondary lymphoid organs

choices.label: E
choices.text: IVIG suppresses CD40 expression so B cells cannot receive Tfh help

explanation.summary: Passively given antibody competes in the germinal center, so no plasma cells or memory B cells are generated until it is cleared.
explanation.whyCorrect: IVIG competes in the germinal center reaction, binding any antigens present on follicular dendritic cells and keeping cognate B cells from accessing the antigen and surviving the GC reaction. Plasma cells and memory B cells are therefore not generated, and the person develops no immunological memory unless they are vaccinated once the IVIG has been cleared. This is why the vaccine is scheduled weeks later.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lymphocyte entry through HEVs is unaffected by IVIG; B cells still enter nodes but cannot win access to antigen on FDCs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IVIG is antibody, not a multivalent antigen; it does not crosslink BCRs or trigger a T-independent response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IVIG persists in the circulation for weeks, which is precisely why vaccination must be delayed; it clearly reaches lymphoid tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IVIG has no described effect on CD40 expression; the block is competition for antigen, not loss of the CD40-CD40L signal.

questions.stem: A patient received a primary immunization 3 weeks ago and now receives a second dose of the same antigen. Within days, serum antigen-specific IgG rises to a level far exceeding the peak of the primary response, and the antibody is of higher affinity. Which of the following properties of the responding cells best accounts for this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are activated by BCR crosslinking without co-stimulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are B1 cells that respond without leaving the marginal zone

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are extrafollicular plasma cells that secrete antibody early

choices.label: D
choices.text: They express surface IgM and IgD and have never seen antigen

choices.label: E
choices.text: They have already class switched and require less T cell help

explanation.summary: Memory B cells drive the secondary response: they need less T cell help and most have already undergone affinity maturation and class switching.
explanation.whyCorrect: A secondary immune response occurs when the immune system encounters an antigen it has seen before, and memory B cells can respond. Memory B cells not only require less T cell help for full activation, but most have gone through affinity maturation and class switching. As a result, not only is more IgG produced, but the overall response is faster and of higher affinity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Activation by BCR crosslinking alone describes T-independent responses, which yield low-affinity IgM rather than rapid, high-affinity IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.B: B1 cells have a low activation threshold but never receive T cell help and secrete predominantly low-affinity IgM, not high-affinity IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Extrafollicular plasma cells are short-lived, produce early IgM in the primary response, and have undergone apoptosis by the time of re-exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cells expressing IgM and IgD that have never seen antigen are naive B cells, which can only mount a slower primary-type response.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old infant presents with a conotruncal cardiac defect, tetany from hypocalcemia, and recurrent viral and fungal infections. A chest radiograph shows an absent thymic shadow. Which of the following processes is most directly impaired in this infant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody class switching in germinal centers

choices.label: C
choices.text: Development of B cells in the bone marrow

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maturation of T cells in the thymus

explanation.summary: The thymus provides the architecture required for T cell maturation, so thymic aplasia (as in DiGeorge syndrome) cripples T cell development.
explanation.whyCorrect: T cell precursors leave the bone marrow and must enter the thymus to mature; the cortex and medulla supply the signals needed for T cell development. Patients with DiGeorge syndrome have little to no thymus and therefore cannot develop T cells properly, leaving them vulnerable to viral and fungal infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Class switching is a germinal-center B cell event and is not the process disrupted by absence of the thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement is a plasma protein cascade unrelated to thymic T cell development.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B cells complete maturation in the bone marrow, which is intact in thymic aplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophil killing is an innate function that does not depend on the thymus.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has a lifelong history of mucocutaneous candidiasis and is later diagnosed with hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in AIRE. In healthy individuals, the AIRE gene product normally enables which of the following?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Costimulation of T cells through CD28 and B7

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive selection of thymocytes in the cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: V(D)J recombination of the T-cell receptor

explanation.summary: AIRE lets thymic medullary epithelial cells display self-antigens from across the genome so self-reactive T cells can be removed by negative selection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Medullary epithelial cells (MECs) use the transcription factor encoded by AIRE to express genes from throughout the genome, including peptides otherwise unique to neurons, the cornea, or the ovaries. This lets self-reactive thymocytes be presented with these antigens and deleted. When AIRE is mutated, negative selection fails and self-reactive T cells escape, producing autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome-1 (APS-1).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Class switching is a B cell process unrelated to thymic tolerance.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28-B7 costimulation is a peripheral priming signal, not a function of AIRE.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Positive selection is carried out by cortical thymic epithelial cells and does not depend on AIRE-driven self-antigen expression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: V(D)J recombination generates the TCR and is independent of AIRE.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: In the thymic cortex, a double-positive thymocyte expresses a rearranged TCR that fails to bind any self peptide-MHC complex. Which of the following is the most likely fate of this cell?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commitment to the CD8+ cytotoxic lineage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Differentiation into a regulatory T cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release into the circulation as a naive helper T cell

explanation.summary: A double-positive cell that cannot bind self-MHC at all fails positive selection and dies by neglect.
explanation.whyCorrect: During positive selection in the cortex, a TCR must bind self-MHC with appropriate affinity to receive survival signals. A cell that does not bind either MHC class I or class II receives no survival signal and undergoes apoptosis, termed death by neglect.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Negative selection deletes cells that bind self-antigen too strongly, not cells that fail to bind at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lineage commitment requires successful binding to self-MHC; a non-binder cannot commit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The regulatory T cell fate is reserved for some strongly self-reactive cells, not for non-binders.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only cells that survive positive and negative selection are released into the circulation.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has extensive treatment-resistant cutaneous warts from human papillomavirus and persistently elevated blood levels of Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in CD28. Which of the following interactions is most directly deficient in this patient?

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD8 binding to MHC class I

choices.label: E
choices.text: TCR binding to the peptide-MHC complex

explanation.summary: CD28 on the T cell must engage B7 on the APC to deliver the costimulatory signal needed for T cell activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Successful priming requires CD28 (on T cells) to engage B7 (CD80/CD86 on APCs) as a costimulatory signal. Loss-of-function mutations in CD28 cause deficient T cell activation, leading to increased viral infections such as severe HPV warts and elevated EBV and cytomegalovirus that healthy adults normally control.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8 binding to MHC class I remains intact and is not encoded by CD28.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LFA-1/ICAM-1 is an adhesion interaction, not the molecule mutated here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PD-1 is an inhibitory receptor; losing it would increase, not decrease, T cell activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TCR binding to peptide-MHC (signal 1) is not affected by a CD28 mutation.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: In the thymic cortex, a double-positive thymocyte expresses a TCR that binds self peptide-MHC class I with appropriate affinity. Into which of the following cells is this thymocyte most likely to differentiate?

explanation.summary: A double-positive cell that is positively selected on MHC class I loses CD4 and becomes a CD8+ cytotoxic single-positive cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: During positive selection, a double-positive cell whose TCR binds MHC class I loses CD4, retains CD8, and becomes a single-positive CD8+ cell committed to the cytotoxic lineage. Binding MHC class I therefore yields a cytotoxic T cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A CD4+ helper cell results from binding MHC class II, not class I.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Double-negative is an earlier, pre-selection stage.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The regulatory T cell fate arises in the medulla from strongly self-reactive cells, not simply from MHC class I binding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Th17 is a peripheral effector subset produced after priming, not a thymic selection outcome.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child presents with abdominal pain and marked peripheral eosinophilia, and stool microscopy reveals helminth eggs. Which of the following CD4+ subsets is most likely driving this response, and which cytokines does it secrete?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Th2 secreting IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13

explanation.summary: Th2 cells drive the response to parasitic worms and secrete IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13.
explanation.whyCorrect: IL-4, secreted by mast cells, dendritic cells, and eosinophils, drives naive T cells toward the Th2 subset. Th2 cells secrete IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and enhance the immune response to parasitic worms (helminths), which fits this child's eosinophilia and helminth infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T cells are CD8+ killers of infected or malignant cells; perforin is not a secreted helper cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Th1 (IFN-gamma, IL-2) targets intracellular pathogens and viruses, not helminths.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Th17 (IL-17) recruits neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tregs suppress immune responses rather than clearing a parasite.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A patient has a disseminated intracellular bacterial infection. Dendritic cells and macrophages at the site secrete IL-12, and nearby NK cells secrete IFN-gamma. Which of the following CD4+ effector subsets is preferentially generated, and what is its main role?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Th2, enhancing eosinophil and antibody responses

explanation.summary: IFN-gamma plus IL-12 drives Th1 differentiation, which enhances defense against intracellular pathogens.
explanation.whyCorrect: IFN-gamma secreted by NK cells and IL-12 secreted by activated macrophages drive naive T cells toward the Th1 subset. Th1 cells enhance the immune response to viruses and intracellular pathogens, matching this scenario.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells and IgE are part of humoral/allergic responses, not the Th1 intracellular defense.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Th17 defends against extracellular bacteria and fungi by recruiting neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Th2 is IL-4-driven and targets helminths and extracellular threats, not intracellular bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tregs dampen responses and would not clear the infection.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 52-year-old kidney transplant recipient is maintained on cyclosporine to prevent rejection. Which of the following best describes the mechanism by which this drug suppresses T cell responses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks CD28 binding to B7

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks the S1P receptor to trap lymphocytes in lymph nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It depletes CD8+ cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It prevents NFAT activation downstream of calcium

explanation.summary: Cyclosporine blocks calcium-dependent activation of NFAT, a transcription factor needed for T cell cytokine production.
explanation.whyCorrect: TCR signaling raises intracellular calcium, which activates the transcription factor NFAT. NFAT (along with NF-kB and AP-1) drives cytokine genes central to T cell activation and proliferation. Cyclosporine blocks the activation of NFAT from increased calcium, dampening the T cell response and preventing rejection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking CD28-B7 costimulation is the mechanism of costimulation blockers, not cyclosporine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Trapping lymphocytes via the S1P receptor is the mechanism of fingolimod.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cyclosporine acts on signaling, not by depleting cytotoxic T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: V(D)J recombination occurs during thymic development and is not the drug target.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis is started on fingolimod. This drug limits disease by interfering with lymphocyte trafficking. Which of the following best describes its mechanism?

choices.label: B
choices.text: It competes with CD28 for B7

choices.label: C
choices.text: It depletes B cells by targeting CD20

explanation.summary: Fingolimod is an S1P receptor 1 modulator that keeps lymphocytes trapped in lymph nodes, preventing them from reaching the periphery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Activated effector T cells normally downregulate CCR7 and upregulate the S1P receptor to follow an S1P gradient out of the secondary lymphoid organs into the circulation. Fingolimod is an S1PR1 modulator that sequesters lymphocytes in lymph nodes, preventing them from carrying out effector functions in the periphery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fingolimod does not act on the IL-2 receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Competing with CD28 for B7 describes CTLA-4-based costimulation blockade.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD20-directed B cell depletion is the mechanism of rituximab, not fingolimod.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibiting NFAT activation describes cyclosporine.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A cytotoxic T cell recognizes a virus-infected cell through its TCR and CD8 co-receptor. Which of the following best describes how the cytotoxic T cell kills this target?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It assembles the complement membrane attack complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: It engulfs the target cell by phagocytosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: It produces antibodies that opsonize the target

choices.label: E
choices.text: It secretes IL-4 to recruit eosinophils

explanation.summary: Cytotoxic T cells kill targets by delivering perforin, which forms membrane pores, and granzymes, which trigger apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytotoxic T cells recognize and kill malignant or pathogen-infected target cells by delivering granules of cytotoxic proteins. Perforin pokes holes in the cell membrane, while granzymes trigger apoptosis. CTLs can also secrete cytokines that activate macrophages and induce inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The membrane attack complex is a complement product, separate from CTL granules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytotoxic T cells induce apoptosis in the target rather than phagocytosing it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibodies are produced by B cells/plasma cells, not T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-4 secretion is a Th2 helper function, not a CTL killing mechanism.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A naive CD4+ T cell circulating in the blood must enter a lymph node to search for its cognate antigen. Which of the following best describes how it gains entry?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds B7 displayed on the venule wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: It crosses high endothelial venules using CCR7

choices.label: D
choices.text: It follows an S1P gradient out of the node

choices.label: E
choices.text: It passes through the thymic corticomedullary junction

explanation.summary: Naive T cells enter lymph nodes across high endothelial venules and home using CCR7.
explanation.whyCorrect: Circulating naive CD4+ and CD8+ T cells enter lymph nodes and other secondary lymphoid organs through specialized high endothelial venules (HEVs) that express high levels of L-selectin ligands and adhesion molecules. Like activated dendritic cells, naive T cells home to lymph nodes using CCR7.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7 is a costimulatory ligand on APCs, not the mechanism of entry across HEVs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Naive T cells use L-selectin (and its ligands on HEVs) to enter; they do not shed it to home in.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Following an S1P gradient drives effector cells out of the node, the opposite direction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The corticomedullary junction is where precursors enter the thymus during development, not how a mature naive T cell enters a lymph node.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: Several days after activation, a T cell upregulates CTLA-4 on its surface. Which of the following best explains how CTLA-4 limits the ongoing T cell response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds peptide-MHC with higher affinity than the TCR

choices.label: B
choices.text: It competes with CD28 for B7, reducing costimulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It induces AIRE expression in the thymus

choices.label: D
choices.text: It secretes IL-2 to expand the response

explanation.summary: CTLA-4 outcompetes CD28 for B7, cutting off the costimulatory signal and dampening the response.
explanation.whyCorrect: CTLA-4 is upregulated on activated T cells and competes with CD28 for B7. By binding B7, CTLA-4 inhibits CD28-mediated costimulation, helping to keep the total number of T cells in check after activation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CTLA-4 binds B7, not peptide-MHC, so it does not compete with the TCR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: AIRE acts in thymic medullary epithelial cells during development and is not induced by CTLA-4.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secreting IL-2 would expand the response, the opposite of CTLA-4's inhibitory effect.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin release is a cytotoxic T cell killing mechanism, unrelated to CTLA-4 inhibition.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A lymphoid progenitor leaves the bone marrow and reaches the thymus to begin maturation. Which of the following best describes the path this cell takes through the thymus before it is released as a mature naive T cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enters at the corticomedullary junction, matures in the medulla, then moves to the cortex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enters at the corticomedullary junction, moves to the cortex, then to the medulla

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enters at the medulla, moves to the cortex, then exits directly from the cortex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enters at the outer capsule, moves through the medulla, then to the cortex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enters through high endothelial venules, matures in the cortex, then exits from the cortex

explanation.summary: T cell precursors enter the thymus at the corticomedullary junction, mature first in the cortex and then in the medulla, and exit from the medulla into the circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: T cell precursors enter the thymus at the corticomedullary junction. Thymocytes then move to the cortex, where they are double-negative and then double-positive, and next to the medulla as they mature into single-positive cells. From the medulla they exit into the circulation as CD4+ or CD8+ mature naive T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Although entry at the corticomedullary junction is correct, cortical maturation precedes medullary maturation, not the reverse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The medulla is the exit point, not the entry point, and cells leave from the medulla rather than the cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Precursors do not enter at the capsule, and the medulla is the last thymic compartment visited, not the first.
whyWrongByChoice.E: High endothelial venules are the entry route into lymph nodes, not the thymus; exit is from the medulla, not the cortex.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A thymocyte in the thymic cortex expresses neither CD4 nor CD8 and has just completed rearrangement of its TCR beta-chain gene. Which of the following receptors is this cell most likely to display on its surface at this stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A complete TCR together with both CD4 and CD8 co-receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: A complete TCR with rearranged alpha and beta chains

choices.label: C
choices.text: A pre-B cell receptor made of a rearranged heavy chain and a surrogate light chain

choices.label: D
choices.text: A pre-TCR made of a rearranged beta chain and a surrogate alpha chain

choices.label: E
choices.text: No antigen receptor of any kind, as in a pro-T cell

explanation.summary: A double-negative pre-T cell expresses a pre-TCR consisting of a rearranged beta chain paired with a surrogate alpha chain.
explanation.whyCorrect: T cells pass through the pro-T, pre-T, and immature stages while they are double-negative (CD4-/CD8-). Pro-T cells express no TCR, pre-T cells express a pre-TCR made of a rearranged beta chain and a surrogate alpha chain, and immature T cells express a full TCR. A double-negative cell that has just rearranged its beta chain is a pre-T cell displaying the pre-TCR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Co-expression of CD4 and CD8 with a full TCR defines the double-positive stage, which the stem excludes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A complete alpha-beta TCR is expressed only at the later immature T cell stage, after the alpha chain has also been rearranged.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pre-B cell receptor with a surrogate light chain belongs to developing B cells in the bone marrow, not thymocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Absence of any receptor defines the earlier pro-T stage, before beta-chain rearrangement.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man recovers from an acute viral illness. Two weeks after the virus has been cleared, the large population of virus-specific effector T cells generated during the infection is markedly reduced. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Effector T cells are converted into B cells by class switching

choices.label: B
choices.text: Effector T cells are sequestered in lymph nodes by S1P

choices.label: C
choices.text: Effector T cells return to the thymus for re-selection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Effector T cells shed their TCRs and revert to naive T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most effector T cells die off once the infection is cleared

explanation.summary: Most effector T cells generated in an immune response die within a couple of weeks after the infection is cleared, leaving a small memory population.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most of the effector T cells generated in an immune response die off within a couple of weeks after the infection is cleared. Only small subpopulations of activated CD4+ and CD8+ T cells differentiate into memory T cells that persist in the circulation, which is why the effector population contracts sharply.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Class switching is a B cell process, and T cells never become B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: S1P is the signal that draws activated T cells out of lymph nodes into the circulation, not one that sequesters them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mature T cells do not return to the thymus; selection occurs only during development.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Effector T cells do not revert to naive cells; naive status is lost once the cell binds its specific antigen.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: During thymic development, V(D)J recombination yields millions of possible T-cell receptors even though the genome contains a limited number of receptor gene segments. Which of the following pairs of mechanisms accounts for this diversity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AIRE-driven gene expression and proteolytic peptide processing

explanation.summary: TCR diversity arises from combinatorial diversity and junctional diversity generated during nearly random V(D)J recombination.
explanation.whyCorrect: V(D)J recombination is almost random, and diversity is generated both by combinatorial diversity (different combinations of gene segments) and junctional diversity (variation at the joints between segments). Together these processes yield millions of possible TCRs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: AIRE expression and proteolytic peptide processing supply self-antigens for selection; they do not diversify the TCR.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Alternative splicing and gene duplication are not the mechanisms the brick describes for TCR diversity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Positive and negative selection test TCRs that already exist; they do not create receptor diversity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatic hypermutation and class switching are B cell processes that occur after antigen encounter, not mechanisms of TCR generation.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: The thymus contains no foreign antigen, yet double-positive thymocytes in the cortex must have their TCRs tested for the ability to bind peptide-MHC. Which of the following is the source of the peptides used for this test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Foreign peptides delivered by dendritic cells that migrate in from infected tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: Immunoglobulin fragments produced by B cells resident in the thymus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peptides derived from the surrogate alpha chain of the pre-TCR

choices.label: D
choices.text: Self-peptides processed by thymic epithelial cell proteases onto MHC I and II

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superantigens that bind MHC outside the peptide-binding groove

explanation.summary: Positive selection uses self-antigen: thymic epithelial cells generate self-peptides with proteases and load them on MHC I and II.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thymus is a sterile place, so TCRs cannot be tested with foreign antigen. Instead, self-antigen is presented by thymic epithelial cells, which use proteases to generate peptides that are loaded onto MHC class I and class II. Double-positive cells that bind these self peptide-MHC complexes weakly receive survival signals during positive selection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick emphasizes that foreign antigen is absent from the thymus, so positive selection cannot rely on it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Immunoglobulin fragments from B cells are not the source of selecting peptides in the thymic cortex.
