whyWrongByChoice.C: The surrogate alpha chain is a component of the pre-TCR, not a source of selecting peptides.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Superantigens are not part of thymic selection; positive selection tests conventional peptide-in-groove binding.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: In the thymic cortex, a double-positive thymocyte binds self peptide-MHC class II with weak, appropriate affinity. Which of the following changes in surface co-receptor expression occurs next in this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It loses both CD4 and CD8 and becomes double-negative

choices.label: B
choices.text: It loses surface CD4 and retains CD8

choices.label: C
choices.text: It loses surface CD8 and retains CD4

choices.label: D
choices.text: It replaces CD4 and CD8 with CD28

choices.label: E
choices.text: It retains both CD4 and CD8 and enters the circulation

explanation.summary: Binding MHC class II during positive selection produces a CD4+ single-positive cell that has lost surface CD8 and is committed to the helper lineage.
explanation.whyCorrect: A double-positive cell whose TCR binds MHC class II becomes a CD4+ single-positive cell, loses surface CD8, and is committed to becoming a helper T cell. This follows the rule of 8: CD4 pairs with MHC class II (4 x 2 = 8), while CD8 pairs with MHC class I (8 x 1 = 8).

whyWrongByChoice.A: Double-negative is the earlier pre-selection stage; a positively selected cell does not lose both co-receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Losing CD4 and keeping CD8 is the fate of a cell that binds MHC class I, which yields a cytotoxic T cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD28 is a costimulatory molecule and does not replace the co-receptors; a single-positive cell retains one of them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cells never enter the circulation as double-positive; they must become single-positive first.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A single-positive thymocyte migrating through the thymic medulla encounters a dendritic cell presenting a self-peptide on MHC. The thymocyte's TCR binds this complex with strong affinity. Which of the following is the most likely outcome?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Conversion back to a double-positive cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Return to the cortex for repeat positive selection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Survival and release as a naive T cell

explanation.summary: Thymocytes that bind self peptide-MHC too strongly in the medulla are destroyed by negative selection to enforce immune tolerance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Single-positive cells that survive positive selection in the cortex migrate to the medulla, where dendritic cells, macrophages, and thymic medullary epithelial cells present self-antigens. Thymocytes that react too strongly to these self-antigens are destroyed by apoptosis in negative selection, which is necessary for immune tolerance and prevention of autoimmune disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Death by neglect occurs in the cortex when a cell fails to bind MHC at all, not when binding is too strong.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Differentiation to single-positive is not reversible; a cell does not regain the second co-receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Thymocytes do not migrate back to the cortex; positive selection is not repeated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Only cells with weak recognition of self peptide-MHC in the medulla survive to become naive T cells.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: In the thymic medulla, a thymocyte whose TCR binds self peptide-MHC strongly is not deleted but instead survives and leaves the thymus. Which of the following cell types has this thymocyte most likely become?

explanation.summary: Some strongly self-reactive thymocytes escape deletion and instead become regulatory T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Strong recognition of self peptide-MHC in the medulla usually triggers apoptosis by negative selection. There is one alternative: some T cells that bind MHC and peptide strongly are not deleted but instead become regulatory T cells, which later inhibit the immune response and help maintain tolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic lineage commitment results from weak binding of MHC class I during positive selection, not strong self-reactivity in the medulla.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Double-negative is the earliest thymocyte stage and is not a fate available to a medullary single-positive cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Memory T cells arise from antigen-activated CD4+ and CD8+ cells in secondary lymphoid organs, not from thymic selection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Th17 cells are an effector subset generated in the periphery after priming under IL-1 and IL-6, not a thymic selection outcome.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 4-month-old girl with DiGeorge syndrome has profound T cell deficiency but normal numbers of hematopoietic stem cells and B cells in the bone marrow. A thymic transplant is proposed. Which of the following best explains why this treatment can restore T cell immunity in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her own bone marrow progenitors are intact and can mature within the transplanted thymus

choices.label: B
choices.text: The graft corrects a V(D)J recombination defect in her developing lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The graft replaces her defective hematopoietic stem cells with donor stem cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The graft restores thymic AIRE expression that is absent in DiGeorge syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: The graft supplies mature donor T cells that directly repopulate her peripheral lymphoid organs

explanation.summary: In DiGeorge syndrome the defect is the missing thymic structure, so a thymic transplant lets the patient's own normal bone marrow progenitors develop into T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients with DiGeorge syndrome have little to no thymus, and without the structure of the thymus T cells cannot develop properly. Their T cell progenitors in the bone marrow are normal. A thymic transplant provides the missing architecture, which allows the T cell progenitors from the bone marrow to develop normally.

whyWrongByChoice.B: V(D)J recombination is intact in DiGeorge syndrome; the problem is the absent thymus, not the recombination machinery.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Her hematopoietic stem cells are normal; a thymus transplant does not replace stem cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: AIRE loss causes APS-1, not DiGeorge syndrome; the DiGeorge defect is thymic aplasia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The benefit comes from providing a maturation environment for the patient's own progenitors, not from delivering donor T cells.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman with APS-1 due to loss-of-function AIRE mutations has autoimmune adrenal failure and hypoparathyroidism despite having circulating regulatory T cells that secrete IL-10. Which of the following best explains why peripheral regulatory mechanisms fail to control her autoimmunity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AIRE is required for regulatory T cells to secrete IL-10, so her own circulating Tregs are nonfunctional

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her self-reactive T cells lack CD28 and therefore cannot be inhibited by CTLA-4 signaling

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her thymus releases only CD8+ T cells, which are not subject to regulatory T cell suppression

choices.label: D
choices.text: IL-10 cannot act on the T cells that were released from a thymus lacking AIRE expression

choices.label: E
choices.text: The number of self-reactive T cells escaping deletion is too large for Treg suppression to compensate

explanation.summary: Without AIRE, potentially all T cells leaving the thymus could be autoreactive, a burden that Treg-mediated suppression cannot overcome.
explanation.whyCorrect: A developing T cell must recognize self-antigen only weakly; strong recognition causes apoptosis. Without AIRE, tissue-restricted self-antigens are simply not expressed in the thymus, so strongly reactive T cells are never given the chance to be deleted. Potentially all of the T cells released from the thymus could be autoreactive, and additional regulatory mechanisms like IL-10 secreted by Tregs cannot compensate for that level of autoimmunity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The stem states that her Tregs secrete IL-10; AIRE acts in thymic medullary epithelial cells, not in Treg cytokine secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nothing in APS-1 removes CD28 from T cells; the defect is in thymic self-antigen expression.
whyWrongByChoice.C: APS-1 affects negative selection of both CD4+ and CD8+ lineages; the thymus does not release only CD8+ cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brick does not describe IL-10 as unable to act on these cells; the failure is one of scale, not of cytokine responsiveness.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A researcher adds a purified bacterial polysaccharide in soluble form to a culture of naive T cells and observes no T cell activation, whereas B cells specific for the same polysaccharide are activated. Which of the following best explains the failure of the T cells to respond?

choices.label: A
choices.text: T cells cannot be activated outside the thymus

choices.label: B
choices.text: T cells express only a single copy of their antigen receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: T cells recognize only antigens that have been bound by antibody

choices.label: D
choices.text: T cells recognize only peptide antigen presented in an MHC complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: T cells require prior class-switch recombination to bind antigen

explanation.summary: T cells are MHC-restricted and recognize only peptide antigen displayed in an MHC complex, unlike B cells, which can bind many antigen types directly.
explanation.whyCorrect: In contrast to B cells, TCRs cannot recognize all types of antigens. T cells are MHC-restricted; they recognize only peptide antigen presented in an MHC complex on an antigen presenting cell. A free polysaccharide is neither a peptide nor MHC-bound, so it cannot engage the TCR, whereas B cells can bind it directly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T cells are activated in secondary lymphoid organs and the periphery, not the thymus; the thymus is for maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Each naive T cell expresses many copies of its single antigen receptor, so receptor number is not the limitation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: T cells do not require antibody-bound antigen; they require peptide presented on MHC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Class-switch recombination is a B cell process and is not a prerequisite for T cell antigen recognition.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A naive CD8+ T cell circulating in the blood enters the spleen to survey for its cognate antigen. Which of the following best describes how this cell reaches the splenic T cell zone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It crosses high endothelial venules expressing L-selectin ligands

choices.label: B
choices.text: It enters at the corticomedullary junction and moves inward

choices.label: C
choices.text: It enters via the open circulatory system, then migrates to the T cell zone

choices.label: D
choices.text: It follows an S1P gradient from the blood into the white pulp

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is carried in by afferent lymphatic vessels from peripheral tissue

explanation.summary: Naive T cells enter the spleen through its open circulatory system and then migrate to the T cell zones, unlike lymph nodes, which are entered across HEVs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Circulating naive T cells enter lymph nodes and other SLOs through high endothelial venules, but the spleen is different. Like B cells, T cells enter the spleen via its open circulatory system and then migrate to the T cell zones to search for antigen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: High endothelial venules with L-selectin ligands are the entry route into lymph nodes, not the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The corticomedullary junction is the thymic entry point for T cell precursors, not part of the spleen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: S1P is higher in blood and lymph than in SLOs, so an S1P gradient draws cells out of SLOs, not into them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Afferent lymphatics are not how the brick describes T cell entry into the spleen; entry is from the blood through the open circulation.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A dendritic cell in a lymph node has taken up debris from apoptotic host cells in the absence of any PAMPs or DAMPs and displays the resulting peptides on MHC class II. A naive CD4+ T cell whose TCR recognizes one of these peptides binds the dendritic cell but is not primed. Which of the following best explains the lack of priming?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Peptides derived from host cells cannot be loaded onto MHC class II

choices.label: B
choices.text: The dendritic cell cannot express MHC class II until it is activated by IL-2

choices.label: C
choices.text: The dendritic cell has not upregulated B7, so CD28 receives no costimulatory signal

choices.label: D
choices.text: The naive T cell has upregulated S1PR1 and already left the lymph node

choices.label: E
choices.text: The naive T cell lacks the CD4 co-receptor needed to engage MHC class II

explanation.summary: Dendritic cells upregulate B7 only after PAMP or DAMP exposure, so without it there is no CD28 costimulation and the T cell is not primed.
explanation.whyCorrect: Following activation by PAMPs and DAMPs, dendritic cells increase costimulatory molecule expression such as B7. A dendritic cell that has not encountered these signals presents peptide-MHC (signal 1) but cannot provide CD28-B7 costimulation. The reliance of T cell activation on CD28 engagement with B7 ensures that T cells are only primed when needed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Host-derived peptides are loaded on MHC; that is how self-peptides are displayed in the thymus and periphery.
whyWrongByChoice.B: MHC class II expression does not depend on IL-2; the dendritic cell in the stem is already displaying peptide on MHC class II.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The stem describes the T cell binding the dendritic cell inside the node, so it has not exited.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A naive CD4+ T cell expresses CD4, and the stem states the T cell binds the dendritic cell; the missing element is costimulation.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: Antigen recognition clusters the TCR complex and co-receptors on a naive T cell. Which of the following proteins directly phosphorylates CD3 to initiate the downstream signaling cascade?

explanation.summary: Lck, a tyrosine kinase associated with CD3, phosphorylates CD3 after TCR clustering; Zap-70 then docks and signals downstream.
explanation.whyCorrect: CD3 is found associated with all TCRs and associates with Lck, a tyrosine kinase, and Zap-70, an adaptor molecule. After the TCR complex and co-receptors are clustered by antigen recognition, Lck phosphorylates CD3. Zap-70 then docks on phosphorylated CD3 and signals downstream, leading to increased cytosolic calcium, PKC, and MAPK activity.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD28 is the costimulatory receptor that binds B7; it is not the kinase that phosphorylates CD3.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NFAT is a transcription factor activated at the end of the cascade by increased cytosolic calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protein kinase C is one of the downstream signaling events that follows Zap-70 docking, not the CD3 kinase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zap-70 is the adaptor that docks on CD3 after phosphorylation; it does not perform the initial phosphorylation.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A naive CD4+ T cell has just been primed in a lymph node by a dendritic cell. Which of the following changes best explains how this cell now sustains its own survival and proliferation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It downregulates CD3 so that the TCR signals continuously without antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: It secretes IL-10 that acts on neighboring T cells to expand the clone

choices.label: C
choices.text: It secretes IL-12 that acts on the dendritic cell to prolong antigen presentation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It upregulates a high-affinity IL-2 receptor and secretes IL-2 that acts back on itself

choices.label: E
choices.text: It upregulates CTLA-4 to increase B7-mediated costimulation from the dendritic cell

explanation.summary: Primed T cells express a high-affinity IL-2 receptor and produce IL-2 themselves, which acts in an autocrine manner to drive survival and proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: IL-2 encourages T cell survival and proliferation following activation. When T cells are primed, they increase expression of a high-affinity IL-2 receptor. IL-2 is produced by the activated T cells themselves and acts in an autocrine manner, feeding back to the cells that secreted it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD3 is required for TCR signaling; downregulating it would impair, not sustain, activation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-10 is a Treg product that suppresses immune responses rather than expanding an activated clone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-12 is secreted by activated macrophages and drives Th1 differentiation; it is not the T cell's autocrine growth signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CTLA-4 competes with CD28 for B7 and reduces costimulation, dampening rather than sustaining the response.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with metastatic renal cell carcinoma is treated with high-dose recombinant human IL-2. Which of the following best describes the intended immunologic effect of this therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blockade of NFAT-driven cytokine transcription in tumor-infiltrating T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into regulatory T cells that quiet tumor inflammation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct induction of Fas-mediated apoptosis in the renal tumor cells by IL-2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Expansion of effector T cell populations, including tumor-directed CD8+ cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sequestration of tumor-reactive lymphocytes within the lymph nodes and spleen

explanation.summary: Recombinant IL-2 expands all effector T cell populations, including CTLs, which then mount an antitumor response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Recombinant human IL-2 is used clinically in the treatment of renal cell carcinoma. Because IL-2 encourages T cell survival and proliferation after activation, it expands all effector T cell populations, including effector CD8+ T cells (cytotoxic T cells), which then mount an antitumor immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking NFAT activation is the mechanism of cyclosporine and suppresses T cells rather than expanding them.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Regulatory T cells inhibit the immune response, which is the opposite of the intended antitumor effect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-2 acts on T cells through the IL-2 receptor; it does not itself kill tumor cells through Fas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sequestering lymphocytes in lymph nodes is the effect of fingolimod, an S1PR1 modulator, and would prevent an antitumor response.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man develops a skin abscess caused by an extracellular bacterium. Dendritic cells and classically activated (M1) macrophages at the site secrete cytokines that direct naive CD4+ T cells toward the subset responsible for enhancing neutrophil recruitment. Which of the following cytokines are most responsible for this differentiation?

explanation.summary: IL-1 and IL-6 from dendritic cells and M1 macrophages drive Th17 differentiation, and Th17 cells secrete IL-17 to enhance neutrophil function.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a classic extracellular bacterial or fungal infection, the IL-1 and IL-6 secreted by dendritic cells and classically activated macrophages (M1s) encourage Th17 differentiation. Th17 cells secrete IL-17, which increases neutrophil infiltration and activation, the appropriate response to extracellular pathogens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma and IL-12 drive Th1 differentiation, which targets viruses and intracellular pathogens rather than recruiting neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-10 and TGF-beta are the effector cytokines of regulatory T cells, which suppress rather than recruit neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 (with IL-2) drives Th2 differentiation for the anti-helminth response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-5 and IL-13 are Th2 effector cytokines involved in worm expulsion and IgE class switching, not Th17 differentiation.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: During resolution of an inflammatory response, alternatively activated (M2) macrophages secrete a cytokine that encourages naive CD4+ T cells to become regulatory T cells. Which of the following correctly pairs that macrophage-derived cytokine with the cytokines the resulting regulatory T cells secrete?

choices.label: D
choices.text: IL-6 and IL-1; IL-17 and IL-22

explanation.summary: TGF-beta from M2 macrophages (and from Tregs themselves) drives Treg differentiation, and Tregs secrete IL-10 and TGF-beta to suppress immune responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anti-inflammatory cytokine TGF-beta, secreted by regulatory T cells and alternatively activated macrophages (M2s), encourages the differentiation of T cells into regulatory T cells. Tregs in turn secrete IL-10 and TGF-beta, producing suppression of immune responses and maintenance of tolerance.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma is a Th1 differentiation and effector cytokine, and IL-17 is a Th17 product, not a Treg product.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-12 from activated macrophages drives Th1 cells, which secrete IFN-gamma and IL-2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-4 drives Th2 differentiation; Th2 cells secrete IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-6 (with IL-1) drives Th17 differentiation; IL-17 is the Th17 effector cytokine.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A CD4+ T cell was primed in a lymph node 3 days ago and is now exiting the node to join the circulating effector cell pool. Which of the following changes in receptor expression enables this exit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Downregulation of CCR7 and upregulation of S1PR1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Downregulation of CD3 and upregulation of CCR7

choices.label: C
choices.text: Upregulation of both CCR7 and S1PR1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Upregulation of CCR7 and downregulation of S1PR1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Upregulation of L-selectin and downregulation of CD28

explanation.summary: Activated T cells downregulate CCR7 and upregulate S1PR1, then follow the S1P gradient out of the SLO into lymph and blood.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sphingosine-1-phosphate (S1P) is present in higher concentrations in lymph and blood than in the SLOs. Activated T cells downregulate CCR7, the receptor that homes them to lymph nodes, and upregulate S1P receptor 1 (S1PR1). They then follow the S1P gradient out of the SLO and enter the circulation with the rest of the effector cell pool.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD3 is retained for TCR signaling, and upregulating CCR7 would keep the cell homed to the node.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CCR7 must fall, not rise, for the cell to leave; keeping CCR7 high would counteract S1P-driven exit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This is the reverse pattern; increased CCR7 would retain the cell in the node and reduced S1PR1 would blind it to the exit gradient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: L-selectin is used for entry across HEVs and for diapedesis, not for exit, and CD28 changes are not the exit signal.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: An effector T cell leaves the blood and enters an infected tissue by diapedesis, using L-selectin, integrins, and cell adhesion molecules. Which of the following events causes the antigen-specific effector cell to be retained at the site of infection rather than continuing to migrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigen recognition promotes integrin binding to the extracellular matrix

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement deposition on the endothelium blocks re-entry into the vessel

choices.label: C
choices.text: Local S1P concentrations fall below those in the surrounding blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: The cell re-expresses CCR7 and homes to the tissue stroma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tissue fibroblasts express B7 and hold the cell through CD28

explanation.summary: Antigen recognition in the tissue activates the effector T cell and promotes integrin binding to the extracellular matrix, retaining the specific cell at the site.
explanation.whyCorrect: At the tissues, T cells enter via diapedesis using the same L-selectin, integrins, and cell adhesion molecules that B cells and neutrophils use. Antigen recognition and subsequent activation then promote integrin binding to the extracellular matrix, which retains the specific effector cells at the site while non-specific cells move on.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement deposition is not the mechanism the brick gives for effector cell retention.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The S1P gradient governs exit from SLOs into lymph and blood; the brick does not describe it as the tissue-retention signal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CCR7 directs homing to lymph nodes and is downregulated on effector cells; it does not anchor them in peripheral tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.E: B7-CD28 is a costimulatory interaction for helper T cell activation, not an adhesion mechanism that anchors cells in tissue.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A hepatocyte infected with hepatitis virus displays viral peptide on MHC class I but does not express B7 (CD80/CD86). Which of the following best describes the ability of primed effector T cells to be reactivated by this cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both cytotoxic and helper T cells can be reactivated because effector cells never need costimulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytotoxic T cells can be reactivated by TCR and CD8 binding alone, unlike helper T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helper T cells can be reactivated by TCR and CD4 binding alone, unlike cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither cytotoxic nor helper T cells can be reactivated without B7 costimulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only memory T cells can respond, because reactivation requires prior antigen exposure

explanation.summary: CTLs are reactivated with TCR and CD8 binding alone, whereas helper T cell reactivation still requires B7-CD28 costimulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the periphery, effector T cells recognize target cells through another immunological synapse in which TCR and co-receptor binding are required. CTLs do not require costimulation through CD28 on reactivation, only TCR and CD8 binding, so a B7-negative infected hepatocyte can still be killed. Reactivation of helper T cells, like initial priming, requires the costimulatory signal of B7 binding to CD28.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Helper T cell reactivation does require B7-CD28 costimulation, so effector cells are not uniformly costimulation-independent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This reverses the rule; it is the cytotoxic cell that can be reactivated without B7, while helper cells require it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This ignores the key difference: cytotoxic T cells do not need CD28 costimulation for reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Effector CTLs, not only memory cells, can respond, and all reactivation still requires TCR engagement of peptide-MHC.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman who had varicella as a child is re-exposed to the virus. Virus-specific memory T cells respond within a peripheral tissue before any T cells have trafficked through a lymph node. Which of the following properties of memory T cells best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are continuously re-selected in the thymus, so their TCRs are already signaling constantly

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are retained permanently within peripheral tissues and never re-enter the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: They express B7 molecules themselves and therefore provide their own costimulatory signal

choices.label: D
choices.text: They lack the CD3 complex and therefore signal without needing any antigen recognition

choices.label: E
choices.text: They need less costimulation and can be activated in tissues without first passing through SLOs

explanation.summary: Memory T cells require less costimulation and can be activated directly in peripheral tissues, so they respond faster than naive T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Memory T cells that were primed by initial exposure to an antigen respond more rapidly to subsequent antigen stimulation than naive T cells. They require less costimulation and can be activated in peripheral tissues without first moving through SLOs, which explains a tissue-level response before any lymph node trafficking.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mature T cells never return to the thymus; thymic selection occurs only during development.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Memory T cells persist in the circulation; they are not permanently fixed in tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B7 is expressed by APCs, not by memory T cells; memory cells simply need less of this costimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD3 is associated with all TCRs and is required for signaling; memory cells still recognize antigen through the TCR.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: During an inflammatory response in the lung, epithelial cells at the site upregulate PD-L1. Which of the following best describes the effect of this expression on activated T cells that have entered the tissue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Displacement of CTLA-4 from B7, increasing T cell activation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enhanced CD28-mediated costimulation, prolonging the T cell response

choices.label: C
choices.text: Induction of Fas on the epithelial cell, causing the epithelium to undergo apoptosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inhibition of costimulation through PD-1, restraining the T cell response at that site

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recruitment of additional naive T cells into the lung through CCR7

explanation.summary: PD-L1 on nonlymphoid tissues engages PD-1 on activated T cells, inhibiting CD28-mediated costimulation and limiting T cell responses at sites of inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: PD-1 is upregulated on activated T cells. Binding of PD-1 by its ligands (PD-L1 and PD-L2) inhibits CD28-mediated costimulation. PD-L1 and PD-L2 on APCs can determine the extent of T cell activation, and PD-L1 expression on nonlymphoid tissues can inhibit T cell responses at sites of inflammation. This is one of the mechanisms that keeps the total number of T cells relatively constant.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Competition with CD28 for B7 is the mechanism of CTLA-4; PD-L1 works through PD-1, not B7.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PD-L1 engagement inhibits rather than enhances CD28-mediated costimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fas/FasL mediates activation-induced death of T cells; PD-L1 does not induce Fas on the epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CCR7 homes naive T cells to lymph nodes; PD-L1 does not recruit naive cells to tissue.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: Several days into an adaptive immune response, activated T cells in a lymph node are observed to undergo apoptosis after contacting one another. Which of the following molecular interactions is most directly responsible for this activation-induced cell death?

choices.label: B
choices.text: FasL binding to Fas on activated T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: IL-2 binding to its high-affinity receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perforin insertion into the T cell membrane

explanation.summary: Activated T cells upregulate Fas, and FasL binding induces apoptosis, so activated T cells expressing both molecules can kill themselves or each other.
explanation.whyCorrect: Activation-induced cell death helps keep the total number of T cells relatively constant. Activated T cells increase expression of Fas, and FasL binding induces apoptosis. Activated T cells that express both Fas and FasL may be killed by themselves or by each other, which explains apoptosis after T cell to T cell contact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CTLA-4 binding B7 blocks costimulation and limits further stimulation; it does not directly trigger apoptosis by cell contact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-2 binding its high-affinity receptor promotes survival and proliferation, the opposite of cell death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PD-1 engagement inhibits CD28-mediated costimulation rather than inducing apoptosis through a death receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin is delivered by CTLs to infected or malignant target cells; it is not the mechanism of activation-induced T cell death.

questions.topicName: T Cell Development, Activation, and Differentiation

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with chronic viral hepatitis undergoes a liver biopsy that shows scattered apoptotic hepatocytes surrounded by CD8+ T lymphocytes, with little surrounding inflammation. One killing mechanism used by these lymphocytes relies on a membrane ligand that engages a death receptor on the target cell, triggering caspase activation. Which of the following molecules mediates this mechanism?

explanation.summary: CTLs kill target cells by perforin/granzyme delivery and by Fas/FasL death-receptor signaling.
explanation.whyCorrect: On activation, CTLs express Fas ligand (FasL). Many nucleated cells display Fas, the receptor for FasL. FasL binding to Fas triggers caspase signaling (including caspase-3) that culminates in apoptosis. Because apoptosis does not release DAMPs, this killing occurs without surrounding inflammation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD16 (FcgammaRIIIA) is an NK-cell receptor for the Fc of IgG used in ADCC, not a CTL death-receptor ligand.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Granzymes enter the cell through perforin pores and activate caspases, but they are not the ligand that engages a death receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Major basic protein is an eosinophil granule protein that kills helminths, not a mediator of CTL death-receptor killing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin polymerizes to form pores in the target membrane; it is not a death-receptor ligand.

questions.stem: An investigator studies how a cytotoxic T lymphocyte kills a melanoma cell it has recognized. After the CTL degranulates, one released protein inserts into and polymerizes within the target cell membrane, creating channels. Which of the following best describes the role of this protein, perforin?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds Fas to initiate death-receptor signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: It directly activates caspases inside the cytosol

choices.label: C
choices.text: It forms pores in the target membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: It recruits neutrophils to the tumor site

explanation.summary: Perforin perforates the target-cell membrane so that granzymes can enter and trigger apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: CTLs secrete perforin and granzymes by exocytosis. Perforin polymerizes in the target cell membrane, perforating it, and granzymes then enter the cell (likely via endocytosis triggered by ion/small-molecule influx through the pores) and activate caspases that drive apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Binding Fas describes the separate Fas/FasL pathway, not perforin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Granzymes, not perforin, activate caspases; perforin's job is to breach the membrane so granzymes can get in.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Toxin neutralization is a humoral (antibody) function, not a role of perforin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophil recruitment is driven by IL-17 from Th17 cells, unrelated to perforin.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with advanced HIV develops disseminated Mycobacterium avium infection. Biopsy shows macrophages filled with acid-fast bacilli that the cells cannot kill. Restoring which of the following cytokines, normally secreted by Th1 cells, would most directly enable these macrophages to destroy the intracellular organisms?

explanation.summary: Th1 cells activate macrophages to kill phagocytosed intracellular pathogens chiefly through IFN-gamma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th1 cells secrete IFN-gamma and express CD40L. IFN-gamma (with CD40L-CD40 engagement) activates the macrophage to produce microbicidal substances in the phagolysosome, including reactive oxygen species and nitric oxide, enabling killing of intracellular organisms such as mycobacteria.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-13 promotes the anti-inflammatory M2 macrophage phenotype and mucus/peristalsis for worm expulsion, not microbicidal activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-17 (Th17) recruits neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi, not intracellular pathogens in macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 is a Th2 cytokine that drives IgE class switching and anti-helminth responses, not macrophage killing of intracellular bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-5 is a Th2 cytokine that activates eosinophils against worms.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant develops disseminated infection shortly after receiving a live attenuated tuberculosis (BCG) vaccine. Genetic testing reveals a loss-of-function mutation in a cytokine receptor whose signaling is required to activate macrophages. A defect in which of the following receptors best explains this presentation?

explanation.summary: IFN-gamma receptor deficiency prevents macrophage activation, so live mycobacterial vaccines can cause severe disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: The TB (BCG) vaccine contains live bacteria similar to Mycobacterium tuberculosis and does not cause disease in healthy individuals. Patients with loss-of-function mutations in the IFN-gamma receptor cannot activate macrophages to kill these bacteria, so the vaccine is contraindicated and can produce severe vaccine-induced infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD16 is an NK Fc receptor for ADCC and has no role in macrophage activation by IFN-gamma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 provides T cell co-stimulation; it is not the receptor through which macrophages are activated to kill intracellular bacteria.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fas is a death receptor used in apoptosis, unrelated to IFN-gamma-driven macrophage activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The IL-4 receptor mediates Th2/IgE responses; its loss would not impair macrophage killing of mycobacteria.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with a history of recurrent skin abscesses, Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, and lung abscesses since childhood. Physical exam shows facial features characteristic of autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome, and genetic testing confirms a STAT3 mutation. Defective differentiation of which of the following T cell subsets best explains her impaired neutrophil recruitment?

explanation.summary: STAT3 loss-of-function impairs Th17 differentiation, reducing IL-17 and neutrophil recruitment against extracellular pathogens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Loss-of-function mutations in STAT3 lead to defective differentiation of naive T cells into Th17 cells. With little IL-17, neutrophil recruitment to infection sites is impaired, so patients suffer recurrent skin and respiratory infections with Staphylococcus aureus and other extracellular pathogens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD8+ CTLs kill infected or malignant cells directly; they do not recruit neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NK cells kill abnormal cells and mediate ADCC; they are not the STAT3-dependent source of neutrophil-recruiting IL-17.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Th1 cells activate macrophages against intracellular pathogens; their loss would not primarily explain defective neutrophil recruitment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Th2 cells target helminths via eosinophils and mast cells, not neutrophil recruitment.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man returns from travel with abdominal discomfort, and stool studies confirm a Strongyloides helminth infection. His complete blood count shows marked eosinophilia. Which of the following Th2 cytokines has the most direct effect on activating eosinophils and promoting their proliferation?

explanation.summary: Among Th2 cytokines, IL-5 has the most direct effect on eosinophils, activating them and driving their proliferation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th2 cells secrete IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 to enhance anti-helminth responses. IL-5 has the most direct effect on eosinophils: it activates them and promotes their proliferation, enabling ADCC-mediated killing of worms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma is a Th1 cytokine that activates macrophages, not eosinophils.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-17 is a Th17 cytokine that recruits neutrophils against extracellular bacteria and fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-2 is a T cell growth factor and is not the Th2 cytokine directly activating eosinophils.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TNF-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine (induced downstream of IL-17) and is not the direct Th2 eosinophil activator.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman with severe allergic rhinitis has elevated serum IgE that arms her mast cells. In the lymph node, a Th2 cytokine induces her B cells to class switch to IgE, which then binds the high-affinity receptor FcepsilonR1 on mast cells and eosinophils. Which of the following cytokines is responsible for this class switching?

explanation.summary: IL-4 drives B cell class switching to IgE, which arms mast cells and eosinophils via FcepsilonR1.
explanation.whyCorrect: IL-4 induces B cell class switching to IgE. IgE binds the high-affinity IgE receptor FcepsilonR1 on mast cells and eosinophils; when antigen cross-links FcepsilonR1-bound IgE, these cells degranulate, releasing mediators such as histamine and toxic granule proteins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma induces class switching to IgG and activates macrophages, not IgE switching.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-12 promotes Th1 responses and does not drive IgE class switching.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-17 recruits neutrophils and does not mediate immunoglobulin class switching to IgE.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-8 is a chemokine that attracts neutrophils, not a driver of IgE class switching.

questions.stem: A virus infecting a patient's cells downregulates surface MHC class I so that CD8+ cytotoxic T cells can no longer detect the infected cells. Which of the following cells is best able to recognize and kill these MHC-I-deficient cells?

explanation.summary: NK cells detect and kill cells that downregulate MHC class I, a strategy virally infected and tumor cells use to evade CTLs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Virally infected and tumor cells often reduce MHC class I to evade CD8+ CTLs, which require peptide-MHC I recognition. NK cells are inhibited by MHC I, so loss of MHC I releases that inhibition and allows NK cells to kill the abnormal cell using perforin and granzymes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells produce antibodies and do not directly kill cells that have lost MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Th1 cells activate macrophages via IFN-gamma; they do not directly kill MHC-I-low target cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD8+ CTLs require peptide-MHC I recognition and are precisely the cells that cannot detect MHC-I-deficient targets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Eosinophils kill helminths via ADCC and granule proteins, not MHC-I-low infected cells.

questions.stem: A patient with lymphoma is treated with a therapeutic IgG monoclonal antibody that coats the tumor cells. Natural killer cells then bind the coated cells and kill them by antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity. Which of the following NK cell receptors recognizes the Fc region of the bound IgG to trigger this killing?

explanation.summary: NK cells perform ADCC using CD16 (FcgammaRIIIA), which binds the Fc region of IgG coating a target cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: In NK-mediated ADCC, CD16 (FcgammaRIIIA) recognizes the Fc region of IgG bound to an infected or malignant cell. CD16 aggregation activates the NK cell to degranulate and kill its target with perforin and granzymes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is a T cell co-stimulatory receptor, not an Fc receptor for ADCC.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FcepsilonR1 is the high-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells and eosinophils, not the NK IgG receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class I is an inhibitory ligand for NK cells, not the receptor that binds IgG Fc.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NK cells do not express an antigen-specific TCR; the TCR is used by T cells to recognize peptide-MHC.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man presents with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia and a recent episode of Cryptococcus meningitis. His CD4+ T cell count is severely reduced. Direct infection and depletion of which of the following cell populations best explains his profound susceptibility to these opportunistic infections?

explanation.summary: HIV infects and depletes CD4+ helper T cells, crippling the coordination of cell-mediated immunity.
explanation.whyCorrect: In HIV/AIDS, infection of CD4+ cells leads to low CD4+ counts and severe immune suppression. Because CD4+ helper T cells are the communicators that coordinate immune responses, their depletion produces susceptibility to AIDS-defining opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii and Cryptococcus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells mediate humoral immunity; their loss does not explain the CD4-driven opportunistic infections seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD8+ CTLs are effector killers, not the cells HIV directly infects and depletes to define AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: NK cells are innate cytotoxic cells and are not the population whose loss defines AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophil defects (e.g., impaired IL-17 recruitment) cause a different pattern of bacterial/fungal abscesses, not the CD4-defined opportunistic picture described.

questions.stem: In an experiment, a naive helper T cell engages a peptide-MHC class II complex through its T cell receptor but receives no B7-CD28 co-stimulatory signal. Which of the following outcomes is most likely for this T cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anergy, a state of functional inactivation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Immediate apoptosis induced by its own perforin

explanation.summary: TCR engagement without B7-CD28 co-stimulation drives a helper T cell into anergy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Helper T cells require both antigen recognition (signal 1) and co-stimulation (signal 2). When TCR engagement occurs in the absence of B7-CD28 binding, the T cell does not activate but instead becomes anergic, a state in which the lymphocyte is functionally inactive and difficult to reactivate.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Class switching is a B cell process driven by cytokines, not the fate of a co-stimulation-deprived T cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anergy is functional inactivation, not perforin-mediated self-killing; helper T cells also do not kill via perforin.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Positive selection occurs during thymic development, not upon peripheral antigen encounter without co-stimulation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Robust activation requires both TCR engagement and B7-CD28 co-stimulation, which is missing here.

questions.stem: A histology study notes that when cytotoxic T cells clear virally infected cells, the surrounding tissue shows minimal inflammation and no damage to neighboring healthy cells. Which of the following best explains why CTL-mediated killing avoids inflammation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apoptosis avoids releasing DAMPs, unlike necrosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complement activation is directly inhibited at the site

choices.label: C
choices.text: CTLs secrete large amounts of anti-inflammatory IL-10

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrophages in the area are globally suppressed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Target cells release histamine that limits swelling

explanation.summary: CTL killing induces apoptosis, which does not release DAMPs, so it does not provoke inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neither the perforin/granzyme nor the Fas/FasL mechanism induces inflammation. Only the target cells marked for destruction are killed, and apoptosis does not release damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) the way necrosis or other damaging cell deaths do, so surrounding tissue is spared.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Complement inhibition is not the mechanism; apoptosis simply does not trigger inflammatory signals.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick attributes the lack of inflammation to apoptosis avoiding DAMP release, not to IL-10 secretion by CTLs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Killing is inflammation-free because of the mode of cell death, not because macrophages are globally suppressed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Histamine release drives inflammation and is a mast cell function, not a reason CTL killing is non-inflammatory.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is found to have a selective defect in cell-mediated immunity with preserved B cell function and normal serum immunoglobulin levels. Which of the following immune functions is most likely to be impaired in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation of complement on bacterial surfaces

choices.label: B
choices.text: Killing of cells infected with intracellular pathogens

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neutralization of free virus particles in serum

explanation.summary: Cell-mediated immunity defends against intracellular pathogens and malignant cells; humoral immunity handles extracellular pathogens.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cell-mediated immunity involves T cells, macrophages, and cytokines and is critical in the defense against intracellular pathogens and malignant cells. CD8+ cytotoxic T cells directly kill infected or malignant cells, so a selective CMI defect most impairs elimination of cells harboring intracellular organisms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Complement activation is a role of immunoglobulins in humoral immunity, not cell-mediated immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Toxin neutralization is a humoral function of immunoglobulins, which are preserved here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neutralization of free pathogens is an antibody function and would remain intact with preserved humoral immunity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opsonization is mediated by antibodies and is part of humoral immunity against extracellular pathogens.

questions.stem: During T cell development, a population of CD8+ T cells is generated whose receptors bind strongly to self-peptides. In a healthy person, which of the following processes prevents these cells from later destroying healthy uninfected tissue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anergy induced in peripheral lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Downregulation of MHC class I on host tissue

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fas-mediated killing by natural killer cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positive selection in the bone marrow

explanation.summary: Self-reactive CD8+ T cells are destroyed by negative selection in the thymus so that CTLs do not kill healthy cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytotoxic T cells must be careful not to destroy healthy uninfected or non-malignant cells. As CD8+ T cells develop, self-reactive cells are destroyed by negative selection in the thymus. The same process removes self-reactive helper T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anergy is a peripheral phenomenon affecting helper T cells that engage TCR without B7-CD28 co-stimulation; it is not the developmental checkpoint that removes self-reactive CD8+ cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Healthy tissue does not protect itself by losing MHC class I; reduced MHC I actually marks a cell for NK killing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NK cells kill abnormal cells that lose MHC class I or express abnormal ligands; they do not police self-reactive T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Selection of developing T cells occurs in the thymus, not the bone marrow, and positive selection does not eliminate self-reactive cells.

questions.stem: A cytotoxic T lymphocyte binds to an influenza-infected respiratory epithelial cell and prepares to release its cytotoxic granules. The viral peptide recognized by the TCR is displayed on the infected cell by which of the following molecules?

explanation.summary: CD8+ CTLs recognize peptide presented on MHC class I, with CD8 acting as the co-receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: CTLs recognize their targets through TCR engagement of a viral peptide displayed on MHC class I, with CD8 binding the MHC I molecule. Once the CTL recognizes and binds its target, it secretes perforin and granzymes by exocytosis to induce apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7 is a co-stimulatory molecule that engages CD28 during priming; it does not display antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD40 is the macrophage or B cell receptor for CD40L on helper T cells; it does not present peptide.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FcepsilonR1 is the high-affinity IgE receptor on mast cells and eosinophils, unrelated to CTL antigen recognition.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peptide-MHC class II complexes are recognized by CD4+ helper T cells, not CD8+ CTLs.

questions.stem: An immunology lecture describes a killing mechanism that is carried out by cells of the innate immune system but depends entirely on antibodies generated by the adaptive immune system. Which of the following pairs of cells mediates this mechanism?

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD8+ T cells and CD4+ T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dendritic cells and follicular helper T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Regulatory T cells and mast cells

explanation.summary: ADCC is mediated by eosinophils and NK cells, innate cells that rely on antibodies from the adaptive response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) is mediated by two types of innate immune cells, eosinophils and NK cells, but relies on antibodies generated by the adaptive immune system. Eosinophils use bound IgE against helminths, and NK cells use IgG recognized through CD16.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells and plasma cells produce the antibodies used in ADCC but do not carry out the cytotoxic killing.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8+ and CD4+ T cells are adaptive lymphocytes that recognize peptide-MHC through the TCR, not antibody-coated targets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dendritic cells prime naive T cells and Tfh cells help B cells; neither performs antibody-dependent killing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tregs regulate immune responses and mast cells degranulate to release histamine; ADCC is attributed to eosinophils and NK cells.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old nursing student undergoes tuberculosis screening with a blood test in which her T cells are removed and exposed to Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigens in vitro. Which of the following is measured to determine whether the test is positive?

explanation.summary: The IFN-gamma release assay (IGRA) measures IFN-gamma released by Th1 cells exposed to TB antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Infection with M. tuberculosis, an intracellular bacterial pathogen, primes and differentiates Th1 cells, which are the main source of IFN-gamma in an immune response. In the IGRA, T cells are removed and exposed to TB antigen, and the IFN-gamma released by TB-specific Th1 cells is measured.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Histamine is released by mast cell degranulation, not by T cells responding to TB antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-17 is the Th17 cytokine that recruits neutrophils; it is not what the TB blood test measures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 is a Th2 cytokine driving IgE switching and is not a readout of Th1 memory to TB.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-5 activates eosinophils against helminths and is unrelated to TB testing.

questions.stem: An investigator engineers mature naive T cells that lack both L-selectin and CCR7 and infuses them into mice. Compared with normal naive T cells, which of the following steps is most likely to be impaired in the engineered cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Entry into lymph nodes through high endothelial venules

choices.label: B
choices.text: Exit from lymph nodes into the circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negative selection of self-reactive clones in the thymus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recognition of peptide-MHC complexes by the TCR

choices.label: E
choices.text: Release of perforin at the immunologic synapse

explanation.summary: Naive T cells home to lymph nodes via HEVs using L-selectin and CCR7.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mature, naive T cells home to lymph nodes via high endothelial venules (HEVs) using L-selectin and CCR7. Without these molecules, naive cells cannot enter the lymph node where dendritic cells prime them with peptide-MHC and CD28/B7 engagement.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Exit from lymph nodes depends on increased S1PR expression by effector T cells, not on L-selectin or CCR7.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Negative selection occurs during development in the thymus and is unrelated to lymph node homing molecules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TCR recognition of peptide-MHC is intact; the defect is in reaching the lymph node where that recognition occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin release is an effector CTL function that occurs after priming and does not depend on L-selectin or CCR7.

questions.stem: T cells that have been primed in a lymph node by dendritic cells are genetically altered so that they cannot increase expression of S1PR. Which of the following is the most likely consequence for these effector T cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They become anergic despite receiving B7-CD28 co-stimulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: They cannot enter lymph nodes through high endothelial venules

choices.label: C
choices.text: They lose the ability to polymerize perforin in target membranes

choices.label: D
choices.text: They remain trapped in the lymph node instead of entering the circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: They undergo negative selection and are destroyed in the thymus

explanation.summary: Effector T cells increase S1PR expression to exit the lymph node and enter the circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Following priming, effector T cells reduce expression of L-selectin and CCR7 and increase expression of S1PR, which allows them to exit the lymph nodes and enter the circulation. Both effector CD8+ CTLs and effector CD4+ Th cells exit the lymph nodes via S1PR, so cells unable to upregulate it cannot leave.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anergy results from TCR engagement without B7-CD28 binding, not from a defect in lymph node egress.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Entry through HEVs depends on L-selectin and CCR7, not S1PR; these cells have already entered and been primed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Perforin polymerization is a cytotoxic granule function unrelated to S1PR.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Negative selection occurs in the thymus during development, not in primed effector cells in lymph nodes.

questions.stem: A tumor cell line is found to resist death-receptor-mediated killing by cytotoxic T cells even though the CTLs express normal levels of their surface death ligand. Sequencing shows the tumor cells have lost a surface receptor that is normally present on many nucleated cells. Loss of which of the following molecules best explains this resistance?

explanation.summary: Fas on the target cell is the receptor for FasL on activated CTLs; its loss blocks death-receptor apoptosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: On activation, CTLs express Fas ligand (FasL) on their membranes, and many nucleated cells have Fas, the receptor for FasL. Binding of FasL on the CTL to Fas on the target triggers caspase signaling (including caspase-3) that leads to apoptosis. A tumor cell that has lost Fas cannot receive this death signal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD8 is the CTL co-receptor for MHC class I; it is not on the target cell.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FasL is the ligand expressed on the activated CTL, and the stem states the CTL death ligand is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MHC class II presents peptide to CD4+ helper T cells and has no role in death-receptor killing of targets.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin is a CTL granule protein used in the separate perforin/granzyme pathway, not a receptor on the target.

questions.stem: In a laboratory study of CTL killing, granzymes are labeled and tracked after cytotoxic granule exocytosis. Which of the following best describes how granzymes gain access to the interior of the target cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Binding to CD16 expressed on the target membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endocytosis triggered by ion influx through perforin pores

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage through channels formed by caspase-3

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transport through the Fas receptor after FasL binding

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uptake through the peptide-MHC class I complex

explanation.summary: Granzymes enter the target cell likely through endocytosis triggered by influx through perforin pores, then activate apoptosis via caspases.
explanation.whyCorrect: After CTLs secrete perforin and granzymes by exocytosis, perforin polymerizes in the target membrane, perforating it. Granzymes then enter the cell, likely through endocytosis triggered by the influx of ions or small molecules through the perforin pores. Once inside, granzymes activate apoptosis through multiple routes, including caspases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD16 is the NK cell Fc receptor for IgG in ADCC and is not on the target cell as a granzyme entry route.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caspase-3 is an intracellular effector activated downstream of granzymes or Fas; it does not form membrane channels.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fas is a death receptor that signals through caspases when bound by FasL; it is not a channel for granzyme entry.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Peptide-MHC class I is recognized by the TCR and CD8 for target identification; it does not internalize granzymes.

questions.stem: A naive CD4+ T cell arrives in a secondary lymphoid organ and begins to proliferate and differentiate into an effector helper T cell. Which of the following best describes the antigen-specific priming signal this cell must receive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD40L presented by an activated B cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgG bound to antigen presented by an NK cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: L-selectin presented by a high endothelial venule

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peptide-MHC class I presented by a macrophage

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peptide-MHC class II presented by a dendritic cell

explanation.summary: Naive CD4+ T cells are primed by dendritic cells in SLOs through peptide-MHC class II plus CD28/B7.
explanation.whyCorrect: Naive CD4+ cells undergo proliferation and differentiation following two critical priming signals provided by dendritic cells in secondary lymphoid organs: binding to a peptide-MHC class II complex and the CD28/B7 interaction. Effector Th cells are then released into the circulation via S1PR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD40L is expressed by activated helper T cells to stimulate B cells and macrophages, not the other way around.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgG on antigen is recognized by CD16 on NK cells during ADCC; it is not a T cell priming signal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: L-selectin is expressed on the naive T cell itself to home through HEVs; it is not an antigen signal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peptide-MHC class I is recognized by CD8+ T cells, not CD4+ helper T cells.

questions.stem: In a lymph node, an activated helper T cell contacts a B cell that has bound its antigen. In addition to cytokines, which of the following contact-dependent signals does the Th cell provide for B cell activation in the humoral response?

explanation.summary: Helper T cells secrete cytokines and, in humoral immunity, provide CD40 stimulation for B cell activation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The main function of Th cells is to secrete cytokines that direct other cells in the immune response. In humoral immunity, they additionally provide CD40 stimulation for B cell activation, a contact-dependent signal delivered through CD40L on the T cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B7 is expressed by antigen-presenting cells to engage CD28 on the T cell during priming, not a signal the Th cell gives the B cell.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD16 aggregation activates NK cells to degranulate during ADCC and has no role in B cell activation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fas engagement by FasL triggers apoptosis of a target cell; it would kill rather than activate the B cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S1PR allows effector T cells to exit lymph nodes; it is not a B cell activation signal.

questions.stem: A macrophage that has phagocytosed bacteria presents bacterial peptide on MHC class II to a Th1 cell. The macrophage has an intact IFN-gamma receptor and receives IFN-gamma, but full activation fails because the Th1 cell cannot express a surface ligand normally induced by TCR engagement. Which of the following ligands is most likely missing?

explanation.summary: Th1 cells activate macrophages through both IFN-gamma and the CD40L/CD40 interaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Binding of the Th1 TCR to its cognate peptide-MHC class II complex on the macrophage triggers the T cell to express CD40L and secrete IFN-gamma. The macrophage recognizes CD40L via CD40 and IFN-gamma via its receptor, and together these signals activate it to produce microbicidal ROS, NO, and lysosomal enzymes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD16 is the NK cell Fc receptor used in ADCC, not a molecule expressed by Th1 cells to activate macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD28 is the T cell receptor for B7 during priming; it is not the ligand that the macrophage recognizes through CD40.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FcepsilonR1 is the IgE receptor on mast cells and eosinophils, not a Th1 surface ligand.
whyWrongByChoice.E: L-selectin mediates naive T cell homing to lymph nodes and is reduced on effector cells; it does not activate macrophages.

questions.stem: After activation by a Th1 cell, a macrophage not only kills the bacteria in its phagolysosomes but also changes its surface phenotype in a way that promotes further Th1 responses. Which of the following changes best accounts for this amplification?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Decreased expression of MHC class I on the surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: Increased expression of CD16 and FcepsilonR1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Increased expression of Fas and FasL on the surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased expression of L-selectin and CCR7

choices.label: E
choices.text: Increased expression of MHC and B7 costimulatory molecules

explanation.summary: Activated macrophages upregulate MHC and costimulatory (B7) molecules and secrete cytokines, promoting further Th1 responses.
explanation.whyCorrect: On activation, macrophages increase cytokine production (TNF, IL-1, IL-12, chemokines) and upregulate MHC and costimulatory molecules such as B7, promoting further Th1 responses. Increased MHC and B7 allow the macrophage to present more peptide and provide co-stimulation to additional T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reduced MHC class I is a strategy of virally infected or tumor cells to evade CTLs, and it would not promote T cell responses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD16 is the NK IgG receptor and FcepsilonR1 the mast cell/eosinophil IgE receptor; neither is described as upregulated on activated macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fas/FasL is the CTL death-receptor pathway, not the mechanism by which activated macrophages amplify Th1 responses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: L-selectin and CCR7 are naive T cell homing molecules, not macrophage activation markers.

questions.stem: During an infection with an intracellular bacterium, B cells in the draining lymph node are exposed to the cytokine that Th1 cells produce in greatest amounts. Which of the following cytokines induces B cells to class switch to IgG in this setting?

explanation.summary: IFN-gamma from Th1 cells induces B cell class switching to IgG, in addition to activating macrophages and CTLs.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th1 cells are the main source of IFN-gamma in an immune response. In addition to activating macrophages, IFN-gamma encourages differentiation of additional Th1 cells, induces B cell class switching to IgG, and activates cytotoxic T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-13 works with IL-4 to increase intestinal mucus and peristalsis and promotes M2 macrophages, not IgG switching.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IL-17 is a Th17 cytokine that recruits neutrophils and does not direct immunoglobulin class switching.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-4 is a Th2 cytokine that induces class switching to IgE, not IgG.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-5 activates eosinophils and promotes their proliferation; it does not direct IgG switching.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man who immigrated from a region with endemic tuberculosis has TB antigens injected intradermally. Two days later, a firm area of induration develops at the injection site. Which of the following best explains the development of this induration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CTLs lysing antigen-bearing target cells with perforin and granzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eosinophils accumulating in response to IL-5 from Th2 cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mast cells releasing histamine after cross-linking of surface IgE

choices.label: D
choices.text: Memory Th1 cells releasing IFN-gamma that activates macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: NK cells degranulating after aggregation of CD16 on IgG-coated cells

explanation.summary: A positive TB skin test reflects reactivation of TB-specific memory Th1 cells, whose IFN-gamma activates macrophages to cause induration.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the TB skin test, injected TB antigens are brought by dendritic cells to the draining lymph nodes. If TB-specific memory Th1 cells are present, they are reactivated, travel to the site, release IFN-gamma, and activate macrophages, causing the induration seen in a positive test.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CTL killing produces apoptosis without inflammation; the induration results from macrophage activation by Th1 cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-5-driven eosinophil accumulation is a Th2 anti-helminth response and is not the basis of the TB skin test.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation is part of the Th2 response to helminths and allergens, not the Th1-driven TB skin test.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NK-mediated ADCC requires IgG-coated target cells and is not the mechanism of a delayed skin reaction to TB antigen.

questions.stem: Mice infected with an intestinal helminth expel the worms through increased intestinal mucus production and peristalsis. Which of the following cytokines acts together with IL-4 to produce these effects?

explanation.summary: IL-13 acts with IL-4 to increase intestinal mucus production and peristalsis to expel worms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th2 cells secrete IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13. IL-13 acts with IL-4 to increase intestinal mucus production and peristalsis to expel worms. IL-13 and IL-4 also promote activation of macrophages to the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IFN-gamma is the Th1 cytokine that activates macrophages against intracellular pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IL-12 is a cytokine secreted by activated macrophages that promotes Th1 responses, not worm expulsion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IL-17 from Th17 cells recruits neutrophils to kill extracellular bacteria and fungi.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-5 has the most direct effect on eosinophils, activating them and promoting their proliferation; it does not drive mucus and peristalsis.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis participates in a study examining CD4+ T cell subsets in central nervous system lesions. The investigators focus on a subset that has been linked to multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and asthma because of its pro-inflammatory properties. Which of the following subsets is being studied?

explanation.summary: Th17 cells are linked to autoimmune diseases such as RA, asthma, lupus, and MS because of their pro-inflammatory properties.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th17 cells secrete IL-17, a family of pro-inflammatory cytokines that induce many other cytokines, chemokines, and prostaglandins. Th17 cells have been linked to many autoimmune diseases including rheumatoid arthritis, asthma, lupus, and multiple sclerosis, likely because of these pro-inflammatory properties.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD8+ CTLs are not a CD4+ helper subset and kill targets by non-inflammatory apoptosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NK cells are innate cytotoxic cells, not a CD4+ T cell subset.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Regulatory T cells differentiate in SLOs but are discussed elsewhere; they are not the pro-inflammatory subset described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Th2 cells enhance anti-helminth responses through IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 and are not the subset linked to these autoimmune diseases.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with a hookworm infection has helminth antigens cross-link IgE bound to FcepsilonR1 on mast cells in the intestinal mucosa, causing degranulation. Which of the following mediators is released from the mast cell granules?

explanation.summary: Mast cell granules contain histamine, tryptase, and eosinophil chemotactic factors; eosinophil granules contain the toxic proteins that kill helminths.
explanation.whyCorrect: When antigens cross-link FcepsilonR1 through IgE, mast cells and eosinophils degranulate. Mast cell granule contents include pro-inflammatory histamine and tryptase as well as eosinophil chemotactic factors. The toxic proteins that directly kill helminths are eosinophil granule contents.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eosinophil cationic protein is one of the eosinophil granule toxins, not a mast cell mediator.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophil peroxidase is an eosinophil granule content, not released by mast cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Eosinophil-derived neurotoxin is an eosinophil granule product that kills helminths.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Major basic protein is an eosinophil granule protein that directly kills helminths, not a mast cell product.

questions.stem: A lymphocyte that lacks an antigen-specific T cell receptor recognizes ligands expressed on the surface of a stressed tumor cell and proceeds to kill it. Which of the following best describes the mechanism this cell uses to kill the tumor cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Expression of CD40L to engage CD40 on the tumor cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Release of major basic protein onto the tumor surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Release of perforin and granzymes that induce apoptosis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secretion of IFN-gamma to activate tumor-associated macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretion of IL-17 to recruit neutrophils to the tumor

explanation.summary: NK cells kill abnormal cells with perforin and granzymes that work exactly like those of cytotoxic T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: NK cells are cytotoxic cells of the innate immune system with the same function as CTLs: killing abnormal (infected or malignant) cells. They recognize ligands that abnormal cells express on their surface, as well as reduced MHC class I expression. On activation, NK cells release granules with perforin and granzymes, which work exactly like the perforin and granzymes of cytotoxic T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD40L is expressed by helper T cells to activate macrophages and B cells; it does not kill tumor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Major basic protein is an eosinophil granule protein that kills helminths, not the NK killing mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IFN-gamma-mediated macrophage activation is the Th1 mechanism against phagocytosed pathogens, not NK cytotoxicity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IL-17 secretion is a Th17 function that recruits neutrophils; NK cells kill targets directly.

questions.stem: During the early response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis in a lymph node, IFN-gamma released by the first differentiated Th1 cells acts on neighboring CD4+ T cells that are being primed. Which of the following effects of IFN-gamma on these cells is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Conversion into CD8+ cytotoxic T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Induction of anergy despite B7-CD28 co-stimulation

explanation.summary: IFN-gamma encourages the differentiation of additional Th1 cells, amplifying the Th1 response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Th1 cells are the main source of IFN-gamma. Beyond activating macrophages, IFN-gamma encourages the differentiation of additional Th1 cells, induces B cell class switching to IgG, and activates cytotoxic T cells. Infection with the intracellular pathogen M. tuberculosis initiates priming and differentiation of Th1 cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4+ helper cells and CD8+ cytotoxic cells are distinct lineages; IFN-gamma activates existing CTLs but does not convert Th cells into them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Th17 differentiation depends on STAT3 and produces IL-17 for neutrophil recruitment; it is not the effect of IFN-gamma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Th2 differentiation enhances anti-helminth responses and is not promoted by the Th1 cytokine IFN-gamma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Anergy occurs when TCR engagement happens without B7-CD28 binding, not as a response to IFN-gamma.

questions.stem: An effector CD8+ T cell that was primed in a lymph node migrates to the lung and encounters a virus-infected epithelial cell displaying viral peptide on MHC class I. The epithelial cell expresses no B7. Which of the following is the most likely outcome of this encounter?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The CTL becomes anergic because B7-CD28 engagement is absent

choices.label: B
choices.text: The CTL fails to kill because the cell lacks MHC class II

choices.label: C
choices.text: The CTL kills the cell because TCR and CD8 engagement suffice

choices.label: D
choices.text: The CTL requires IgG on the target to engage CD16

choices.label: E
choices.text: The CTL waits for Th17-derived IL-17 to recruit neutrophils

explanation.summary: Unlike helper T cells, effector CTLs do not require CD28 co-stimulation for reactivation in the periphery, only TCR and CD8 binding.
explanation.whyCorrect: Priming of naive CD8+ T cells requires TCR, CD8, and CD28/B7 engagement, but effector CD8+ T cells (CTLs) do not require co-stimulation through CD28 for reactivation in the periphery, only TCR and CD8 binding. Once the CTL recognizes and binds its target, it secretes perforin and granzymes to induce apoptosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anergy from absent B7-CD28 binding applies to helper T cells, which must receive the same activation signals for reactivation; CTLs are exempt.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CTLs recognize peptide on MHC class I, which the infected cell displays; MHC class II is irrelevant to CTL killing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD16-mediated recognition of IgG is the NK cell ADCC mechanism, not a requirement for CTL killing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CTL killing is direct and does not depend on IL-17-mediated neutrophil recruitment.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman is recovering from a tissue-invasive helminth infection.
